poll78.assessment: Three traps walked into in one fire, two of them already written down in this very file, by an agent that had read the file's key list but not those entries before acting. The recurrence rate is not improving. The durable fix is not 'read harder' -- it is to make the correct forms executable rather than prose: a single canonical endpoint+schema accessor and a canonical selector map, consumed by every site. That is the Syntactic-Semantic Seam Rule applied to this project's own tooling, and it should be an explicit deliverable of the camera-control work.

poll82.whatRecurred: Three previously-recorded traps were all walked into again within a single cold fire, in sequence, before any of them was recognised: the /v2/Common/ path prefix (HTTP 200 + HTML, surfacing as a jq numeric-literal error at column 26), .Session.Competitors instead of .SortedCompetitors (silent length 0), and .SessionID/.SessionEpoch being null (silent wrong sort). Each cost one round trip.
poll82.whyItKeepsHappening: Every one of these is the NAME A REASONABLE PERSON WOULD GUESS. The API's real names are the unusual ones (GroupedSessions, SortedCompetitors, SessionStartDateEpoc). A cold agent reconstructs the plausible name from the endpoint's own title, not from the recorded schema, unless it reads the schema FIRST.
poll82.procedureFix: Read apiSessionSchemaFieldTraps, apiWrongKeySilentZero, apiEndpointPathTrap and apiGroupedSessionsTopLevelKeyTrap BEFORE issuing the first API call of a fire, not after the first parse failure. Better still, keep a single canonical extractor snippet in the summary doc so no fire re-derives the field names -- this is a textbook single-source-of-truth failure, currently re-solved from scratch every cold start.
poll82.note: Recorded here rather than treated as a mere annoyance because it is directly predictive of how a future automated ingestion agent will behave on its own cold start.

apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.problem: Within one real on-track session, the API can expose 2-3 sibling records sharing (Name, CategoryString). Blue Sprint 1: 8720237 (epoch 1786199705, 21 cars, stub), 8720238 (epoch 1786200139, 18 cars, stub), 8720307 (epoch 1786200139, 19 cars, REAL 21-lap final). Yellow Sprint 1: 8720318, 8720319, both stubs so far.
apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.whyEpochFails: 8720238 and 8720307 share the SAME epoch 1786200139, so sort-by-epoch is a tie and may return the stub. Epoch cannot discriminate stub from final, period.
apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.candidateRule: Group by (Name, CategoryString); within the group take the highest ID; then VALIDATE the record by content before accepting it -- specifically that maxLaps is plausible for the session's configured duration (today: ~30 min at ~1:26-1:36 lap times => ~19-21 laps). Highest-ID would have selected 8720307 correctly for Blue.
apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.residualGap: Highest-ID alone is NOT sufficient: for Yellow right now it selects 8720319, a 2-lap stub, because the real final has not published yet. The maxLaps plausibility check is what converts that from a wrong answer into a correct 'not ready yet, keep polling'.
apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.status: CONFIRMED 2-for-2 (upgraded from CANDIDATE at poll 53). Blue Sprint 1 -> 8720307 (21 laps, correct); Yellow Sprint 1 -> 8720472 (21 laps, correct, matches the widget final exactly). In both cases highest-ID-within-(Name,CategoryString) selected the real final and the maxLaps plausibility check correctly rejected the 2-lap stubs. Still to re-test against the three Sprint 2 sessions.
apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.poll53Resolution: The residualGap noted at poll 47 is now CLOSED for Yellow. At poll 47 highest-ID selected 8720319, a 2-lap stub, and the maxLaps plausibility check correctly returned not-ready-yet rather than a wrong answer. At poll 53 the real final 8720472 published and highest-ID selected it. This is the rule working as designed across the not-ready -> ready transition, which is the case that actually matters for an ingestion consumer.
apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.epochIsNotPublishTime: NEW at poll 53, and it kills epoch as a selection key for a SECOND independent reason. 8720472 carries epoch 1786202567 = 11:22:47, one second after stub 8720319s 1786202566 = 11:22:46 -- yet 8720472 did not exist in the listing at 13:03 and appeared by 13:09:30. The epoch field encodes something session-start-shaped, NOT the records publication time, so it cannot order records by recency either. Combined with the Blue Sprint 1 exact-epoch tie (8720238 and 8720307 both 1786200139), epoch is unusable for stub-vs-final discrimination in both the tied and the untied case.
apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.poll55ThirdConfirmation: Re-ran the rule cold at 13:23. Group by (Name, CategoryString) over all 29 sessions, take highest ID, then content-validate: for Yellow Sprint 1 it selects 8720472 (28 competitors, maxLaps 21, leader #320 CUNICELLI best 00:01:26.916), which matches the widget's final classification exactly. Third consecutive correct selection. The record has been byte-stable since it appeared at poll 53, consistent with final-results records being written once and then immutable -- the same one-shot-write behaviour as the stubs, differing only in that the content is correct.
apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.poll63FiveSiblingGroup: The documented '2-3 sibling records' upper bound is WRONG. Practice 1 Red has FIVE siblings sharing (Name, CategoryString): 8718672/8718674/8718675/8718679/8718696. The grouping key itself held up fine -- all five grouped correctly -- so the rule's KEY is unaffected; only the stated cardinality was too low. More importantly the five members are progressive mid-session snapshots with monotonically rising maxLaps (2, 4, 4, 5, 10), which reframes what siblings are; see apiProgressiveSnapshotChain, including the newly-identified gap where the maxLaps plausibility check cannot separate 'not finalised yet' from 'never finalised'.

poll66_fourthConfirmation_AND_A_NEW_GAP.confirmation: Ran the rule cold at 14:48 over all 32 sessions. For Blue Sprint 2, group (Name='Sprint 2', CategoryString='911CUP / E / GT4 / SP2 / SP3 / VGTO / VO / VU') contains {8720631, 8720632}; highest ID = 8720632; content-validate -> maxLaps 8, implausible for a ~30-min session, so the rule correctly returns NOT-READY-YET rather than a wrong answer. Fourth consecutive correct behaviour.

newGap_cautionShortenedSessionsBreakTheP.problem: The plausibility check is documented as 'maxLaps is plausible for the session's configured duration (today: ~30 min at ~1:26-1:36 lap times => ~19-21 laps)'. Blue Sprint 2's TRUE final is 16 laps, because a caution ended it 5m13s early. That is OUTSIDE the documented band. When the real final publishes, this check will REJECT it and the rule will report not-ready-yet forever.
newGap_cautionShortenedSessionsBreakTheP.whyThisWasInvisibleUntilNow: The band was calibrated on Blue Sprint 1 (21 laps) and Yellow Sprint 1 (21 laps), both full-distance. Today's first caution-shortened session is the first case that falls outside it. This is exactly the CLAUDE.md threshold-boundary failure mode: a numeric band derived from the cases the author had seen, with no test at or below its lower edge.
newGap_cautionShortenedSessionsBreakTheP.proposedFix: Replace the absolute-laps band with a STUB-RELATIVE test, because the stub's own maxLaps is knowable at query time and the session's actual run length is not. Candidate: accept a record as final when maxLaps >= max(3 * stubMaxLaps, stubMaxLaps + 5), which would accept 16 against a stub of 8 and still reject the stub itself. UNTESTED -- registered here as a proposal, not a validated rule, and the constants are guesses. A second, cheaper discriminator worth combining: the widget's retained post-session grid gives the true lap count directly, so a system that scrapes the widget anyway can validate the API record against it and needs no heuristic band at all.
newGap_cautionShortenedSessionsBreakTheP.status: OPEN. Testable when Blue Sprint 2's real final publishes -- watch for a third sibling with maxLaps 16.

poll79_STUB_RELATIVE_PROPOSAL_DISPROVEN.severity: HIGH -- falsifies the concrete constants proposed at poll 66, before they could be written into an ingestion consumer.
poll79_STUB_RELATIVE_PROPOSAL_DISPROVEN.theProposal: poll66.newGap_cautionShortenedSessionsBreakThePlausibilityBand proposed replacing the absolute-laps band with a stub-relative test: 'accept a record as final when maxLaps >= max(3 * stubMaxLaps, stubMaxLaps + 5)', explicitly flagged UNTESTED with guessed constants.
poll79_STUB_RELATIVE_PROPOSAL_DISPROVEN.theTest: Blue Sprint 2 is the case it was designed for. Its stub maxLaps is 8 and its TRUE final is 16 laps (caution-shortened). The proposed threshold evaluates to max(3*8, 8+5) = max(24, 13) = 24. A true final of 16 is BELOW 24, so the rule would reject the correct record and report not-ready-yet FOREVER.
poll79_STUB_RELATIVE_PROPOSAL_DISPROVEN.verdict: DISPROVEN as specified. The 3x multiplier is the offending term: it is calibrated on full-distance sessions (stub 2 laps -> final 21 laps is a 10x ratio) and has no validity when the stub is captured late in a session that then ends early. The stub's lap count is not a fixed fraction of the final's -- it depends on when the snapshot happened to be taken, which is exactly the quantity that varies wildly (see apiProgressiveSnapshotChain).
poll79_STUB_RELATIVE_PROPOSAL_DISPROVEN.newEvidenceThisFire: Blue Sprint 2 grew a THIRD sibling this fire, 8720882, with maxLaps 13 -- still short of the true 16, and published roughly 1h51m after its 14:40:57 checkered. So the chain is 8 -> 8 -> 13 and still has not converged. Any rule keyed on a ratio to the FIRST stub is chasing a moving denominator.
poll79_STUB_RELATIVE_PROPOSAL_DISPROVEN.whatToDoInstead: Abandon heuristic lap-count bands. The poll-66 entry already named the correct answer and it should be promoted from an aside to the rule: a system that scrapes the widget anyway ALREADY KNOWS the true final lap count from the retained post-session grid, so it should validate the API record against that observed value and accept the record when they agree. This needs no constants, no calibration, and degrades correctly on caution-shortened sessions. Heuristic bands should be used only by a consumer that has no widget access at all, and such a consumer should be documented as unable to distinguish 'not finalised yet' from 'never finalised'.
poll79_STUB_RELATIVE_PROPOSAL_DISPROVEN.residualOpenItem: Whether Blue Sprint 2 ever publishes a 16-lap record at all is still unknown, and today's capture will likely end before it resolves. Worth a single follow-up query on a later day -- it is the difference between 'the publish lag is long' and 'caution-shortened sessions are never correctly finalised', which are very different problems for an archival consumer.

apiStubEpochPairPattern.discovered: 2026-08-08T12:48-04:00 (poll 49), by converting the sibling epochs for BOTH Sprint 1 sessions and comparing them against the widget-derived green times
apiStubEpochPairPattern.observation: Each Sprint session publishes a PAIR of stub records whose SessionStartDateEpoc values land in two distinct, repeatable places: (a) the SCHEDULED session start, to the minute, and (b) roughly three minutes AFTER the actual green.
apiStubEpochPairPattern.whyItMatters: This explains MECHANICALLY why sort-by-epoch cannot discriminate stub from final. Blue final 8720307 carries epoch 1786200139 -- EXACTLY stubB (8720238) epoch, not a later one. The final does not get a fresh timestamp; it inherits a stub epoch, producing a genuine tie that any max-by-epoch selector resolves arbitrarily. Combined with apiFinalResultsSelectionRule the practical consequence is unchanged: group by (Name, CategoryString), take the highest ID, then CONTENT-VALIDATE via maxLaps plausibility.
apiStubEpochPairPattern.secondaryUse: stubA epoch is a usable proxy for the PUBLISHED SCHEDULE (it tracks the posted time, not the green) and stubB epoch is a usable proxy for GREEN MINUS ~3 MIN. Neither is a live signal -- both only become visible well after the fact -- but for offline reconstruction of a race day they are more informative than they first look.
apiStubEpochPairPattern.caveat: Sample size 2, same day, same timing operator. The ~3min offset on stubB is NOT established as a constant; treat it as an observed range, not a formula. Re-test on the Sprint 2 sessions before relying on any part of this.

poll51ContentAsymmetry.discovered: 2026-08-08T12:57-04:00 (poll 51), by pulling SessionDetails for all four stub siblings and histogramming Laps and LastLapTime rather than reading only the leader row
poll51ContentAsymmetry.observation: The stub PAIR differs in a reproducible CONTENT shape, not just in ID and epoch. The lower-ID sibling carries LastLapTime on nearly every competitor and retains entries whose Laps field is blank; the higher-ID sibling has LastLapTime stripped to ~zero and drops one or more rows.
poll51ContentAsymmetry.reproduced: 2 of 2 Sprint sessions, same polarity both times (lower ID = fuller field + LastLapTime present; higher ID = smaller field + LastLapTime absent).
poll51ContentAsymmetry.consequenceForSelection: This is a trap for any 'pick the record with more data' heuristic: by field count and by LastLapTime coverage the LOWER-ID stub looks strictly better, yet neither stub is the answer -- for Blue the correct record is 8720307, the HIGHEST ID, with maxLaps=21. Richness heuristics and ID-ordering heuristics point opposite ways here, and only the maxLaps content check resolves it.
poll51ContentAsymmetry.discardedInference: An earlier reading this same fire -- that the higher-ID stub's competitor count tracks the widget's leaderboard row count at teardown -- was checked and DISCARDED: Blue's widget teardown row count was 19, its higher-ID stub is 18, and its real final 8720307 is 19.

poll51EpochIsALabelNotACaptureTime.finding: SessionStartDateEpoc does NOT indicate when the snapshot was taken. Blue Sprint 1 stubA (8720237) carries epoch 1786199705 = 10:35:05, which is the SCHEDULED start and is 4m17s BEFORE the 10:39:22 green -- yet its content already shows 18 competitors with 1 completed lap, data that could not exist before roughly 10:40:50 (green + one ~1:26 lap). Content therefore postdates the record's own epoch by ~6 minutes.
poll51EpochIsALabelNotACaptureTime.correctsWhat: The 'secondaryUse' note above remains valid as stated -- stubA epoch tracks the posted schedule and stubB epoch tracks green+~3min -- but ONLY as session-start LABELS. Do not read either epoch as the instant the competitor data was sampled; both siblings are early-session snapshots (leader on lap 1-2) that are then frozen permanently.
poll51EpochIsALabelNotACaptureTime.whyItMatters: A consumer reconstructing a race day offline could otherwise timestamp stub competitor data at the record epoch and get lap-completion times that precede the green flag.

apiStubEpochPairPattern.poll52EpochKeyIsMisspelled: SCHEMA CORRECTION: the epoch key is spelled 'SessionStartDateEpoc' -- no trailing 'h'. This fire's first query used '.Epoch' and got a column of nulls with HTTP 200, Content-Type application/json and .Successful==true: it failed exactly like every other documented trap here -- silently, and in a way that reads as 'this race has no session timestamps' rather than 'you typed the wrong key'. Full verified Session key list, in order: ID, RaceID, Name, SessionDate, SessionTime, SortMode, Categories, CategoryString, ResultsProcessorVersion, SessionStartDateEpoc. Note that SessionDate and SessionTime are BOTH null on all 29 session records for this race -- SessionStartDateEpoc is the only usable timestamp, so the two plausibly-named date fields are decoys that a schema-guessing client will reach for first.

apiCompetitorFieldSemanticsTrap.finding: SortedCompetitors rows carry TWO fields whose names do not describe their contents, and one plausible field that does not exist at all.
evidence: Leader row of stub 8720319 verbatim: {"FirstName":"DAVID","LastName":"CUNICELLI",...,"Nationality":"SILVER","AdditionalData":"P 14 CAYMAN S","Category":"1"}
The widget's second display line for each car ('SILVER / P 14 CAYMAN S', 'BLUE / 70 911') is exactly Nationality + ' / ' + AdditionalData.
traps: 'Nationality' holds the LIVERY / PAINT SCHEME, not a nationality: values observed include SILVER, BLUE, YELLOW, BLACK/GREEN, BLUE/WHITE/RED, WHITE/ORANGE, MULTI, PURPLE.
'AdditionalData' holds the CAR DESCRIPTION (year + model, sometimes prefixed 'P '), not arbitrary extra data.

There is NO '.Name' field. Querying .SortedCompetitors[0].Name returns null silently -- FirstName and LastName are separate. This is the FIFTH distinct silent-null field trap recorded today (after .Groups, .SessionID, .SessionDate, .Session.Competitors).

'Category' is the integer-as-string '1' for every row -- it is NOT the class code. The class shown by the widget (J, SPC, SPB, ME1, G, I) is NOT present anywhere in the competitor row; it is only derivable from the session-level CategoryString, which lists the group's classes but does not map cars to them.
apiCompetitorFieldSemanticsTrap.whyItMatters: This is the MECHANISM behind textGrepIsInsufficient. The livery false-positive floor that defeats any body-text color-word flag detector is not incidental page noise -- it is a first-class data field ('Nationality') that the timing operator populates with colour words for every car in the field, and the widget renders verbatim. The floor is therefore structural and permanent, not a rendering artifact that might be filtered away.
apiCompetitorFieldSemanticsTrap.durableRule: Per the CLAUDE.md syntactic-semantic seam rule, do not infer a field's semantics from its name in this API. Nationality must be ingested as a livery string; any consumer treating it as a country code will silently store paint schemes. And per the data-capture rule, enumerate the row's actual key set (18 keys, listed in apiCompetitorSchema below) rather than allow-listing from assumed names.
apiCompetitorFieldSemanticsTrap.severityForCameraControl: Positive as well as negative: livery colour is exactly the kind of attribute a camera-control/auto-tagging layer wants per car, and it turns out to be available structurally rather than needing to be parsed out of the rendered second line.

apiCompetitorSchema.verifiedAcross: all 28 rows of stub 8720319 and all 19 rows of real final 8720307
apiCompetitorSchema.typeNote: All scalar fields are STRINGS including Position, Laps, BestLap, Category (extends apiFieldTypesAreStrings to the competitor object). ID, SessionID and RaceID are the exceptions -- genuine integers.
apiCompetitorSchema.note: No key was null anywhere in either record -- the failure mode in this API is the EMPTY STRING, not null (extends apiBlankNumericFields). Nulls only appear when you ask for a key that does not exist.

apiLapTimesArrayIsAlwaysEmpty.finding: Every competitor row carries a 'LapTimes' array. It is EMPTY in every row of every record inspected -- including the confirmed real-final record for a completed 21-lap session.
apiLapTimesArrayIsAlwaysEmpty.evidence: Stub 8720319 (28 rows, maxLaps 2): all LapTimes []. Real final 8720307 (Blue Sprint 1, 19 rows, maxLaps 21, TotalTime 00:30:51.202 on the leader): sum of LapTimes lengths across all 19 rows = 0, max = 0.
apiLapTimesArrayIsAlwaysEmpty.whyItMatters: This is a schema-shaped invitation to a data source that does not exist. An extractor written against the schema would plausibly plan to reconstruct per-lap history (and therefore lap-by-lap pace, traffic, and stint structure) from LapTimes, and would find it empty only at runtime, on real data, with no error raised -- an empty array is indistinguishable from 'this session had no laps'. Per-lap history is NOT retrievable from this API for this race; the only per-lap information available is the aggregate triple (Laps, LastLapTime, BestLap/BestLapTime), and LastLapTime is itself empty on 27/28 rows of an in-progress stub.
apiLapTimesArrayIsAlwaysEmpty.consequenceForCameraControl: Any desire for lap-by-lap timing must be satisfied by POLLING THE WIDGET at a cadence finer than a lap (~1:26-1:36 here, so <=30s to be safe) and differencing successive snapshots. It cannot be backfilled from the archive afterwards. This is a hard argument for capturing at speed DURING a session rather than relying on post-session reconciliation.
apiLapTimesArrayIsAlwaysEmpty.caveat: Single race, single timing operator, ResultsProcessorVersion 4. It is possible LapTimes is populated for other events or operators. Do not generalise beyond 'empty here, and empty on a finished session, so not something to depend on'.

apiNoProvisionalFlag.question: Is there any METADATA field that marks an API session record as a provisional/in-progress stub rather than a completed final?
apiNoProvisionalFlag.answer: No. Checked ResultsProcessorVersion, SortMode, SessionDate and SessionTime across all five Sprint 1 records -- the four stubs (8720237, 8720238, 8720318, 8720319) and the one confirmed real final (8720307). All five are byte-identical on these fields: ResultsProcessorVersion=4, SortMode='race', SessionDate=null, SessionTime=null.
apiNoProvisionalFlag.consequence: This upgrades the content check in apiFinalResultsSelectionRule from 'prudent belt-and-braces' to 'the only mechanism that exists'. There is no flag to read, no version bump, no timestamp that advances on finalization. A consumer MUST validate maxLaps against the session's plausible lap count and treat an implausibly low value as 'not published yet, keep polling' rather than as a result.
apiNoProvisionalFlag.relatedRule: This is the No Log Scraping / structured-signaling problem seen from the consumer side: the producer publishes no typed 'provisional vs final' condition, so the consumer is forced to infer state from payload content. Worth recording as a concrete example of why that rule matters -- the inference here (maxLaps plausibility) needs an out-of-band fact (the session's configured duration and typical lap time) that the API never supplies.

apiTransientEmptyBody.observation: A loop issuing three back-to-back POSTs to /v2/Results/SessionDetails (8720307, 8720318, 8720319) writing to files got a full 7290-byte body for the first and ZERO-BYTE bodies for the other two. curl exited 0 on all three. Refetching each individually seconds later returned complete, correct JSON.
apiTransientEmptyBody.reproductionAttempt: NOT REPRODUCED. A deliberate 6-request rapid loop over the same three IDs returned HTTP 200 with the expected byte counts 6/6 (7290/10881/10207, ~0.14s each), and a 3-request loop at 1s spacing likewise returned 3/3 complete. So this is not a simple per-second rate limit, and the mechanism is unidentified.
apiTransientEmptyBody.confidence: OBSERVED ONCE, NOT REPRODUCED. Recorded because the failure mode matters more than its measured frequency -- NOT because the cause is understood. Do not build a retry policy around an assumed rate limit; that would be inventing a mechanism this data does not support.
apiTransientEmptyBody.whyItMatters: An empty body is the one failure the existing validation chain does not catch on its own terms: the HTTP status is 200, and the .Successful check cannot run because there is no JSON to check. A client that treats a JSON-parse failure as 'no data yet' -- which is precisely how three of the six poll-47/poll-50 trap recurrences presented -- would silently report an empty session. Same user-visible signature as the /v2/Common/ path trap, entirely different cause.
apiTransientEmptyBody.durableRule: Assert a NON-EMPTY response body as its own explicit precondition, BEFORE the Content-Type check and before .Successful -- and type an empty body as a retryable transport fault, never as 'the session has no competitors'. This is the CLAUDE.md No-Log-Scraping rule applied to an API client: 'transport gave me nothing' vs 'the server says there is nothing' must be a typed branch, not an inference from where a parser happened to fail.

fieldSizeIsPerSessionNotPerRunGroup.finding: Red Sprint 1 armed with 23 cars. The Red Warm-Up had 9. Full day: Blue 14 -> 21, Yellow 19 -> 29, Red 9 -> 23. Every run group's sprint field is substantially larger than its warm-up field, and Red's is a 2.6x jump.
fieldSizeIsPerSessionNotPerRunGroup.whatItInvalidates: The poll-51 nextExpectedSession prediction that Red Sprint 1 would show a SHORT arm window because 'Red has been the smallest field of the day (9 cars)'. That premise was drawn from the Red WARM-UP and does not carry to the sprint. The prediction was retired on contact, before it could be scored.
fieldSizeIsPerSessionNotPerRunGroup.effectOnTheArmDurationHypothesis: The field-size-drives-arm-duration hypothesis is NOT refuted -- it simply was not tested by this session the way poll 51 intended. Red Sprint 1's 23 cars sits between Blue Sprint 1 (21 cars, 34s arm) and Yellow Sprint 1 (29 cars, 3m02s arm), so its arm duration is still a usable interpolation test; the arm bracket here is 3m18s wide, which is too coarse to score it. To actually test the hypothesis you need a sub-minute cadence around the scheduled start, not a 5-minute one.
fieldSizeIsPerSessionNotPerRunGroup.durableRule: Treat field size as a property of the SESSION, never of the run group. Do not carry a car count forward from one session to the next even within the same run group and the same day. Combined with the already-established 'row count varies in both directions WITHIN a session', the conclusion is that no car count is stable enough to key anything on -- not session identity, not run group, not field size. Run group is identified by the leaderboard class tokens and nothing else.

lastSeenSessionIdNote: 8721134 is the NEWER of two in-progress FROZEN stubs for the live Red Sprint 2 (the other is 8721133). Neither is a final result -- both report maxLaps 6 while the widget leader is on lap 12. Do not read lastSeenSessionId as 'the current state of the session'; it is only the newest API record ID seen.

runGroupIdentificationByClassTokens.why: The stop condition requires identifying Red Sprint 2. The session-name field is useless for this (reads bare 'Sprint 1'/'Sprint 2' for all three run groups), so class tokens are the only discriminator. Prior state-file guidance said to match 'by class tokens (GT3/GTB1/GTC3/...)' -- that phrasing is UNSAFE and this poll shows why.
runGroupIdentificationByClassTokens.finding: CategoryString (API) and the leaderboard class column (widget) are a per-session CENSUS of the classes actually present, NOT a fixed run-group roster. They shrink when fewer classes turn up.

evidence.api_allThreeGroups: Every one of the 29 API sessions was checked. Red: Practice/Qualifying publish all 11 tokens (GT3/GTB1/GTC3/GTC5/GTC6/GTC7/GTC8/GTD1/GTD2/GTD3/STG) but the Red Warm-Up (8720222, 9 cars) publishes only 'GT3 / GTB1 / GTD2' -- 3 of 11. Blue: Sprint 1 publishes 8 tokens but the Blue Warm-Up (8720136) publishes 7, dropping E. Yellow: Sprint 1 publishes 6 but the Yellow Warm-Up (8720158) publishes 5, dropping I. Three-for-three, the Warm-Up string is a proper subset of the same group's race string.
evidence.widget_thisPoll: Red Sprint 1's 19 running rows carry only 8 distinct class tokens (GTB1,GTC3,GTC5,GTC6,GTC7,GTC8,GTD1,GTD2). GT3 and STG were present in the 24-row arm-order grid at poll 53 and are absent from the running field; GTD3 has not appeared in a Saturday session at all. So the census shrinks not just between sessions but between ARM and GREEN within one session.
evidence.disjointnessCheck: Computed over all 29 sessions: the six distinct CategoryStrings collapse to exactly three MAXIMAL token sets, and all three pairwise intersections are EMPTY. Every observed CategoryString is a subset of exactly one maximal set, with zero violations.

runGroupIdentificationByClassTokens.durableRule: Match on ANY-token-membership in a run group's universe, never on presence of a specific token and never on the full set. Because the three universes are provably disjoint, a single observed class token is sufficient and unambiguous to identify the run group. A matcher keyed on 'contains GTC*' would have MISCLASSIFIED the Red Warm-Up (GT3/GTB1/GTD2, no GTC token at all) as not-Red; a matcher requiring the full 11-token Red set would have matched nothing on Saturday at all.
runGroupIdentificationByClassTokens.relationToClaudeMdRules: This is the Syntactic-Semantic Seam Rule in its canonical form: the semantic distinction is 'which run group is on track', and it must live in one canonical data structure (the three disjoint token universes above) that both the widget scraper and any API consumer CONSUME. Neither site should re-encode the rule as its own substring or prefix test.
runGroupIdentificationByClassTokens.caveat: The universes are derived from one race weekend's entry list and are specific to this event's class structure. They are NOT portable to another club race. A production camera controller should derive the universes at event start from the Practice/Qualifying sessions -- which publish the fullest rosters -- and then verify disjointness before relying on single-token matching. If a future event's groups are NOT disjoint, single-token matching is invalid and the whole approach needs revisiting.

poll75_apiCategoryStringIsMoreStableThan.observation: Yellow Sprint 2's widget class census read G/I/J/ME1/SPB/SPC (6 tokens) on the 29-row grid at poll 74 and reads G/J/ME1/SPB/SPC (5 tokens) on the settled 20-row grid at poll 75. Class I disappeared entirely because BOTH of its entries (#315 DAN MATTHEWS, #501 CLIFF GOLDSMITH) were non-starters and were culled. The API's CategoryString for the SAME session still reads all six tokens including I.
poll75_apiCategoryStringIsMoreStableThan.whyItMatters: This is a sharper version of the caveat already recorded here. The census does not merely shrink -- it can drop a class to ZERO representation, which means a matcher looking for a SPECIFIC token can fail even when the run group is unambiguously on track. The existing durableRule (match on ANY-token membership in a disjoint universe) survives this intact and is vindicated: any one of G/J/ME1/SPB/SPC still identifies Yellow correctly.
poll75_apiCategoryStringIsMoreStableThan.sourcePreference: For run-group identification prefer the API CategoryString (entry roster, stable) or the ARMED widget grid (full entry list) over the running widget census (starters only, shrinks). Where only the running census is available, ANY-token matching is mandatory, not merely advisable.
poll75_apiCategoryStringIsMoreStableThan.stopConditionImplication: Directly relevant to identifying Red Sprint 2. Do NOT wait to see a specific Red token such as GT3 or STG -- Red Warm-Up already published only GT3/GTB1/GTD2 of 11, and this fire shows the running census can lose classes outright. A single observed token from the Red universe is sufficient and is the intended test.

greenInstantDerivationIsDriftFree.finding: Red Sprint 1's green instant has now been derived three times from independent captures spread across 9m44s of the session, all landing on 13:08:07 exactly: 13:08:40-00:00:33, 13:10:24-00:02:17, and 13:17:57-00:09:50.
greenInstantDerivationIsDriftFree.whyItMatters: The widget's session clock does not drift measurably against its own displayed wall clock over at least a ten-minute window. So the green instant can be recovered by clock arithmetic at ANY point during a green session, not only from a capture taken near the transition. For a 5-minute-cadence poller that will routinely miss the green edge itself, this converts a missed transition from a lost data point into a recoverable one.
greenInstantDerivationIsDriftFree.limits: Both operands come from the same header render, so this establishes internal consistency, not agreement with an external time source -- it does not license using the widget clock as a wall-clock reference for camera timestamps. It also says nothing about behavior across a yellow/full-course-caution period, which has not occurred today; a clock that pauses under caution would break the derivation and has not been ruled out.
greenInstantDerivationIsDriftFree.poll76: 9th consecutive zero-drift derivation for Yellow Sprint 2: 16:02:14 - 00:19:48 = 15:42:26, identical to the value derived at 15:43:49, 15:53:04, 15:53:52, 15:54:06 and 15:56:51. Derivation has now held across a 19-minute span within one session with no rounding walk, confirming the widget's Timing clock and its wall clock are driven from the same source rather than independently.

poll79_SETTLED_AND_EXTENDED_ACROSS_A_CAU.statusChange: Red Sprint 2's green instant was recorded at poll 78 as PROVISIONAL, explicitly requiring 'two further zero-drift re-derivations'. It has now had SEVEN, so 16:22:58 is SETTLED.
poll79_SETTLED_AND_EXTENDED_ACROSS_A_CAU.theMoreImportantResult: Four of the seven straddle a full-course caution and a restart. The limits clause of the parent finding said in as many words: 'it says nothing about behavior across a yellow/full-course-caution period, which has not occurred today; a clock that pauses under caution would break the derivation and has not been ruled out.' That gap was partially closed at poll 65 for a caution that ran into the Finish; it is now closed for a caution that RESTARTS, which is the harder case because a restart is where a pause-and-resume implementation would most plausibly reveal itself. The clock does not pause, does not skip, and does not re-baseline at the restart.
poll79_SETTLED_AND_EXTENDED_ACROSS_A_CAU.independentCorroboration: clock + ttg summed to exactly 00:29:59 on all seven probes against a 00:30:00 configured duration -- the same one-second offset seen all day, unchanged by the caution. So the two header fields stayed mutually consistent as well as individually drift-free.
poll79_SETTLED_AND_EXTENDED_ACROSS_A_CAU.remainingLimit: Unchanged and still worth stating: both operands come from the same header render, so this establishes internal consistency, not agreement with an external time source. It does not license using the widget clock as a wall-clock reference for camera timestamps.

poll81.drift: ZERO on all three. Running total: 13 consecutive drift-free derivations of the Red Sprint 2 green instant, spanning a full-course caution and a restart.
poll81.invariantHeld: clock + ttg = 00:29:59 on all three probes (21:45+08:14, 21:59+08:00, 24:28+05:31), matching the configured 30:00 duration less the widget's one-second display convention.
poll81.forwardProjectionAgreement: The three probes independently project ttg->0 at 16:52:57, agreeing to the SECOND. Six independent derivations across two fires now agree on that instant. The session clock is therefore a high-quality predictor and can be trusted to schedule a probe cadence around the expected checkered -- while remaining, per projectedNextCheckered, not a stop signal in itself.

poll82.result: green re-derives as EXACTLY 16:22:58 at all 8 hold probes (clock 00:31:49/00:32:13/00:33:08/00:33:58/00:34:17/00:34:45/00:35:07/00:35:27 against the widget's own wall clock). Zero drift, ~36 minutes after green.
poll82.throughTheHold: The clock kept advancing at real-time rate through the entire post-checkered hold and passed the configured 00:29:59 without any state change -- reconfirming poll65's clockRunsPastConfiguredDuration on a second session, and on a NORMAL full-distance finish rather than a caution-shortened one.
poll82.acrossACaution: This session contained a full-course caution and a restart (16:28:49 / 16:30:11) and the derivation is still drift-free across them, consistent with poll 79. The clock is a pure since-green wall counter, unaffected by caution, restart, checkered, or the configured duration elapsing.
poll82.atTeardown: The clock RESET to 00:00:00 at 16:59:49, which is the only thing all day that has ever perturbed it.

apiInProgressStubIsNotGuaranteed.discovered: 2026-08-08T13:24-04:00 (poll 55), by testing the poll-49 stub-pair pattern against its first out-of-sample session
apiInProgressStubIsNotGuaranteed.falsifies: apiStubEpochPairPattern's implicit generalization that 'each Sprint session publishes a PAIR of stub records', which held 2-for-2 (Blue, Yellow) and is now 2-for-3.
apiInProgressStubIsNotGuaranteed.observation: Red Sprint 1 went green at 13:08:07. At 13:22:27 (green + 14m20s) the API listing still contains exactly 29 sessions and NOT ONE of them carries a Red CategoryString newer than the 09:54 Warm-Up (8720222). There is no stubA, no stubB, and no final for Red Sprint 1 -- the session is entirely invisible to the API while running.
apiInProgressStubIsNotGuaranteed.contrastEvidence: Both prior Sprint sessions had visible in-progress stubs well before this point in their run: Blue Sprint 1's siblings 8720237/8720238 were being read at elapsed 00:09:28 (poll 23), and Yellow Sprint 1's 8720318/8720319 at elapsed 00:07:06 (poll 31). Red is now at 00:14:20 with nothing at all. The absence is therefore not merely 'earlier in the sequence' -- it is past the point where both prior sessions had already published.
apiInProgressStubIsNotGuaranteed.epochCaveat: Per poll51EpochIsALabelNotACaptureTime, SessionStartDateEpoc is a session-start LABEL, not a publish time, so stubs for Red Sprint 1 could still appear later carrying backdated ~13:05 and ~13:11 epochs. That would NOT rescue the pattern as a live signal: it would only confirm that stub APPEARANCE time is unbounded in the same way final-results appearance time already is (apiFinalResultsPublishLagIsUnbounded).
apiInProgressStubIsNotGuaranteed.durableRule: Do not treat 'a session record exists in the API' as evidence that a session has started, and do not treat its absence as evidence that one has not. Presence in the results listing is uncorrelated with live on-track state in BOTH directions -- stale records persist for sessions long finished, and running sessions can be wholly absent. This closes the last plausible reading in which the API could contribute anything to live session detection.
apiInProgressStubIsNotGuaranteed.openItem: Watch whether Red Sprint 1 stubs appear at all, and if so with what epochs. If they appear with ~13:05/~13:11 epochs, that pins the epoch-as-backdated-label model. If Red Sprint 1 skips straight to a single final-results record with no stubs, the stub pair is an artifact of specific sessions rather than a per-session convention.
apiInProgressStubIsNotGuaranteed.poll57Escalation: Red Sprint 1 is now at 00:23:44 elapsed -- roughly 80% through its 30-minute window and within ~6 minutes of its checkered -- and the API listing STILL contains exactly 29 sessions with no Red record newer than the 09:54 Warm-Up (8720222). Elapsed-time-with-zero-API-presence has now been extended 14:20 -> 20:13 -> 23:44 across polls 55/56/57. Blue Sprint 1 had a visible stub at 09:28 and Yellow Sprint 1 at 07:06, so Red is now at ~2.5x and ~3.4x those thresholds respectively. The stub PAIR pattern is 2-for-3 and the weaker claim 'a running session eventually appears while running' is now 2-for-3 as well.
apiInProgressStubIsNotGuaranteed.openItemStatus: The poll-55 open item is still open but narrowing: if Red Sprint 1 publishes nothing before its checkered, the observation upgrades from 'stubs are not guaranteed early' to 'stubs may never appear at all for a session', and the stub pair is confirmed an artifact of specific sessions rather than a per-session convention. Watch the next 2-3 fires specifically for whether Red Sprint 1 skips straight to a single final-results record.

leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips.discovered: 2026-08-08T13:23-04:00 (poll 55), from two widget captures 16 seconds apart within a single poll
leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips.observation: The Diff and Gap cells are not a single data type. For a car on the lead lap they hold a numeric seconds string ('26.595'); for a lapped car they hold a lap-count PHRASE. At 13:22:27 P4 #636 DORIA (9 laps, leader on 10) read Diff='+1 lap' / Gap='+1 laps'; at 13:22:43, having completed lap 10, the same car read Diff='53.637' / Gap='25.681'.
leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips.secondaryTrap: The two columns do not even agree on the phrase: Diff uses the SINGULAR '+1 lap' while Gap uses the PLURAL '+1 laps', for the same car in the same render. A parser keyed on one column's exact wording will fail on the other.
leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips.leaderRowTrap: P1's Diff and Gap cells are EMPTY, not zero. Three distinct value shapes therefore occupy one column: empty (leader), numeric seconds, and a lap phrase.
leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips.whyItMatters: This is the CLAUDE.md Syntactic-Semantic Seam Rule in a data-capture skin: 'how far back is this car' is one semantic quantity encoded in three syntactic forms that switch on lap-down status, and the switch can happen between two reads 16 seconds apart. A float() over the column silently throws or -- worse, with a permissive regex -- extracts the bare 1 from '+1 lap' and records a 1-second gap for a car a full lap down.
leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips.durableRule: Parse Diff/Gap into a tagged value (LEADER | SECONDS float | LAPS_DOWN int), never into a bare float. Test all three forms plus the singular/plural variance explicitly; per the Threshold-Boundary rule, the lapped-car case is exactly the ambiguous input that must be pinned by a test rather than assumed away.
leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips.alsoNote: Independent of the type flip, this pair of captures re-confirms that the leaderboard mutates continuously: #125 DEBUSMANN fell P5 -> P7 in the same 16 seconds. Any consumer must treat a single read as a point sample, not as a session state.
leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips.poll67_intraGridFlip: 2026-08-08T14:58:34-04:00, Blue Sprint 2 hold: rows 19 (#08 JUSTIN JACOBS) and 20 (#525 DAMON DeCASTRO) both read Laps=9, four laps down on the 13-lap leader, yet render Diff/Gap with DIFFERENT TYPES -- '+4 laps / +1 laps' vs '8:28.311 / 8:28.311'. Previously this finding described the type flipping between polls; it also flips BETWEEN ROWS OF A SINGLE RENDERED GRID at identical lap deficits. Consequence: a consumer must parse the gap column's type PER ROW and must not sniff it once per capture and apply it grid-wide.

poll69.newInstance: #525 DAMON DeCASTRO, 9 laps in both readings, rendered a TIME gap '8:28.311 / 8:28.311' at 14:58:34 and LAP-COUNT gaps '+4 laps / +2 laps' at 15:12:38. The type flip is for the SAME CAR at the SAME LAP COUNT across a rewind step.
poll69.prior: Poll-67-correction established the type can flip BETWEEN ROWS of one grid. This extends it: the type also flips for one row ACROSS grids without its lap count changing.
poll69.consequence: The Diff/Gap columns are type-unstable along both axes. A parser MUST classify each cell's type at read time (does it match /^\+?-?\d+ laps?$/ vs a time literal) rather than assuming a column type. Do not coerce these to a numeric seconds value without a type tag.

classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.severity: HIGH -- this is a defect in the STOP CONDITION's own discriminator, found by instrumenting it rather than trusting it.
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.relationToPriorFinding: runGroupIdentificationByClassTokens (poll 54) established WHICH tokens identify a run group and proved the three universes are pairwise disjoint. That finding is unchanged and still correct. This finding is about WHERE the tokens are read from, which poll 54 never pinned down -- and the obvious reading site is wrong.
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.whatHappened: This fire matched the three run-group universes against document.body.innerText with whitespace-bounded regexes. Result: redTok = 8 tokens (correct), yelTok = [] (correct), blueTok = ['GT4'] -- a FALSE POSITIVE in a session with zero Blue cars.
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.rootCause: 'GT4' occurs twice in the body text, both times inside the car-MODEL string in the .additionalData field: #45 DAVID FELKER 'RED/WHITE/BLUE / 16 981 CAYMAN GT4 CLUBSPORT' and #125 PETER DEBUSMANN 'GREEN/BLACK / 16 981 CAYMAN GT4 CLUBSPORT'. Both cars' ACTUAL class, read from .racerCategory, is GTD1 -- a RED-universe token. A Porsche 981 Cayman GT4 Clubsport is simply a car whose model name collides with the Blue group's GT4 class token.
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.whyTheDisjointnessProofDoesNotSaveYou: The poll-54 disjointness proof is a statement about the CLASS-TOKEN VOCABULARY: no token belongs to two run-group universes. It says nothing about the surrounding prose. Model names, livery strings and driver names are an unbounded vocabulary that freely collides with the class vocabulary. Disjointness of the universes does NOT make body-text matching safe, and the poll-54 durableRule ('a single observed class token is sufficient and unambiguous') is only true of tokens read from the class field.
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.howItWouldHaveFailed: Under the ANY-token-membership rule a body-text matcher sees a Blue token in a pure-Red session. Depending on how ties are broken it either misclassifies Red Sprint 1 as Blue, or flags the session as ambiguous/multi-group. Either way the stop condition -- 'is this Red Sprint 2?' -- becomes unreliable at exactly the moment it has to be right. Worse, it is silent: nothing about the observed output looks wrong unless you print the per-universe token lists, which is only why this was caught.
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.correctExtraction: Per leaderboard row, the class token is the textContent of the row's .racerCategory child. Structured extraction over the 19 rows this poll returned exactly {GTB1,GTC3,GTC5,GTC6,GTC7,GTC8,GTD1,GTD2}: 8 Red, 0 Blue, 0 Yellow, 0 unknown -- clean, with the GT4 false positive gone. Row DOM shape confirmed this poll: .racerRowStacked > .positionContainer > .position, then .racerRowItem.row1 > .racerName + .racerCategory, then .row1.additionalData (livery/model), then .racerRowItem.row2 (labels) and .racerRowItem.row3 (values).
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.singleLetterTokensAreALatentLandmine: The Blue universe contains the single-letter token 'E' and the Yellow universe contains 'G', 'I' and 'J'. Against body innerText these are catastrophically ambiguous -- they will match initials, livery abbreviations and stray words. This poll's whitespace-bounded regexes happened not to fire on them in a Red session, which is luck, not safety. Reading .racerCategory makes the single-letter tokens exact-match-safe because the element contains the class token and nothing else. This is an additional, independent reason the extraction site must be structural.
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.relationToClaudeMdRules: Textbook Syntactic-Semantic Seam Rule: the semantic distinction is 'which class is this car in', and it must be read from the one element that carries it. Grepping the page for the token re-encodes the distinction as a substring test over a document that contains a much larger, uncontrolled vocabulary. Structurally identical to the poll-46 driver-name finding in textGrepIsInsufficient ('JaRED' contains 'red'), and to that finding's warning that adding word boundaries is a partial mitigation that LOOKS like a fix: whitespace boundaries removed nothing here, because 'GT4' is already a whole token inside the model string.
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.durableRule: Extract run-group class tokens ONLY from the per-row .racerCategory element. Never from document.body.innerText, never from a row's innerText (which concatenates racerName + racerCategory + the model/livery string), and never from the API's CategoryString when a widget read is available. Then apply the poll-54 any-token-membership test to that structured set. Assert the extracted set is non-empty and that its cross-universe intersections are empty; a token appearing in two universes' match lists means the extraction site is wrong, not that the universes overlap.
classTokenExtractionSiteTrap.verification: Both extraction sites run side by side in the same page state this poll. Body-text: 8 Red + 1 spurious Blue. Structured .racerCategory: 8 Red + 0 Blue + 0 Yellow + 0 unknown. The two disagree, and the structured one is right.

gapColumnCanBeNegative.extends: leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips (poll 55), which catalogued THREE shapes for Diff/Gap: EMPTY (leader), SECONDS, and a lap PHRASE. This adds a FOURTH shape and, more importantly, breaks the implicit assumption that the lap phrase is non-negative.
gapColumnCanBeNegative.observation: P19 #44 JOE MANSFIELD read Diff='+3 laps' and Gap='+-2 laps' -- a double-signed literal, '+' immediately followed by '-2'.
gapColumnCanBeNegative.rootCause: Diff is measured to the LEADER; Gap is measured to the CAR AHEAD BY POSITION. The leaderboard order is NOT strictly by lap count: P18 #125 DEBUSMANN was on 9 laps while P19 #44 MANSFIELD was on 11. So Gap for #44 computes (9 - 11) = -2, and the widget's formatter unconditionally prefixes '+' to a lap-count gap, yielding the literal '+-2 laps'. Diff, computed against the 14-lap leader, is a well-formed '+3 laps'. Both cells are internally consistent with their own definitions; only the formatter is wrong.
gapColumnCanBeNegative.whyPositionAndLapCountDisagree: HYPOTHESIS, NOT CONFIRMED: #44's last lap read 03:36.788 (roughly 2.5x a normal 01:22-01:26 lap), consistent with a pit stop or an off. substringClassSelectorDoubleCount.severity: MEDIUM -- it did not corrupt this poll's answer, but only because a set-dedup happened to absorb it. Any count-based or per-row logic would have been exactly 2x wrong, silently.
substringClassSelectorDoubleCount.whatHappened: This fire's DOM probe selected leaderboard rows with document.querySelectorAll('[class*="racerRow"]') and then filtered to those containing a .racerCategory descendant. It returned 38 nodes for a leaderboard that visually and structurally has 19 rows.
substringClassSelectorDoubleCount.rootCause: The substring 'racerRow' matches BOTH the row container class 'racerRowStacked' AND its inner class 'racerRowItem'. Per the row DOM shape recorded in classTokenExtractionSiteTrap, each row is .racerRowStacked > ... > .racerRowItem.row1 > (.racerName + .racerCategory), so the container and its .row1 child BOTH match the selector, and because querySelector('.racerCategory') searches DESCENDANTS, both also pass the 'contains a category' filter. Exactly 2 matches per row, 19 rows, 38 nodes.
substringClassSelectorDoubleCount.whyItWasNotCaughtByTheOutput: The extracted class tokens were pushed through a Set, so the duplicate reads collapsed and the token universe came out correct (8 Red, 0 Blue, 0 Yellow, 0 unknown). The ONLY visible symptom was the rowCount field reading 38 against a get_page_text capture showing 19 positions. Had the probe not also printed a raw count, the defect would have been invisible.
howItCouldBite: Any per-row aggregate -- mean lap time, count of cars on the lead lap, count of retirements -- is computed over each row twice.
leaderboardRowCountIsNotFieldSize already forbids using row count for field size or session identity; this adds that the DOM count is not even a reliable count of ROWS unless the selector is exact.
A future consumer diffing rowCount across polls to detect leaderboard churn would see a doubled baseline and mis-scale any threshold built on it.
substringClassSelectorDoubleCount.correctSelector: Select rows by EXACT class: document.querySelectorAll('.racerRowStacked') (narrow branch) or the wide-layout equivalent, resolved by reading the actual row class first -- do NOT hardcode 'racerRowStacked', since stackedLayoutAndZeroViewportCaveat records that the layout branch depends on viewport width. Then read the category with a scoped query from that container. Verify the count against the highest rendered position number, which is an independent witness.
substringClassSelectorDoubleCount.relationToClaudeMdRules: Syntactic-Semantic Seam Rule, substring-test form, and it is the same shape as classTokenExtractionSiteTrap from the previous fire: the semantic distinction is 'is this element a leaderboard ROW', and a substring test over the class attribute re-encodes that distinction against an uncontrolled vocabulary -- here the site's own sibling class names rather than driver or livery prose. Two consecutive fires have now produced a substring-matching defect in the SAME extraction path, which suggests the path needs one canonical row-and-field accessor that every probe consumes, rather than ad-hoc selectors written per poll.
substringClassSelectorDoubleCount.durableRule: Never select DOM nodes for this widget with [class*=...] or any substring/prefix class match. Use exact class matching, and cross-check the resulting row count against the maximum rendered position number before using it for anything. If the two disagree, the selector is wrong -- do not reconcile by deduplicating, which hides the defect.
substringClassSelectorDoubleCount.verification: Same page state: get_page_text renders positions 1..19; the substring selector returned 38; 38 == 2 x 19 exactly, and the per-row DOM shape accounts for both matches.

javascriptToolSamplingLoopBudget.why: Two attempts this fire to bracket the checkered with a tight in-page sampling loop both died on a tool timeout, costing the tightest measurement of the day at the exact moment it mattered.
javascriptToolSamplingLoopBudget.finding: [REVISED AT POLL 63 -- see CORRECTION_poll63; the 1.410 throttle FACTOR below is DISPROVED] mcp__Claude_Browser__javascript_tool enforces a hard 30s cap. async/await IS supported and correctly awaited (verified: a promise-returning IIFE resolved normally). But setTimeout inside the HIDDEN Browser pane is THROTTLED.
javascriptToolSamplingLoopBudget.measurement: A control loop of 5 samples with 4 x 2000ms nominal sleep (8000ms nominal) took 11287ms wall. Throttle factor 1.410.
failures: 12 samples x 1.9s = 20.9s nominal -> ~29.5s throttled -- timed out despite being comfortably under 30s NOMINAL. This is the instructive one.
javascriptToolSamplingLoopBudget.durableRule: [REVISED AT POLL 63 -- the <=15s nominal budget below is TOO GENEROUS; use ~8s. See CORRECTION_poll63] Budget in-page sleep at <= ~15s NOMINAL (~21s throttled) per javascript_tool call. Never size a sampling loop from nominal sleep alone -- multiply by ~1.4 for the hidden-pane throttle, then leave headroom for page-script and serialization overhead.
javascriptToolSamplingLoopBudget.alternative: For windows longer than ~15s, chain several short in-page loops across successive tool calls rather than one long loop. Each call's round-trip (~18-60s observed today) is itself the coarse sampling interval, so the in-page loop is only worth using to get FINE resolution inside one call.
javascriptToolSamplingLoopBudget.relationToPriorMethod: Supersedes the ad-hoc 'take a deliberate second capture inside one fire' technique used at polls 27 and 28. That worked, but its resolution was the tool round-trip. A compliant in-page loop gives ~2s resolution within a 15s window, which is what the flagLeadsLeaderboard discriminating experiment needs.

CORRECTION_poll63.severity: MEDIUM-HIGH -- the documented budget rule is wrong in BOTH directions and caused three tool timeouts this fire.
CORRECTION_poll63.whatTheDocumentedRuleSaid: 'setTimeout in the hidden pane is THROTTLED by a factor of 1.410; budget in-page sleep at <= ~15s NOMINAL (~21s throttled) per javascript_tool call; a compliant loop gives ~2s resolution within a 15s window.'

errorOne_throttleIsQuantizationNotAFacto.measurement: 250ms nominal sleep -> gaps [1062, 1000, 1000, 1002, 998, 1001] ms, mean 1011ms. The multiplicative model predicts 375ms; a +1000ms additive model predicts 1250ms. Neither fits. 900ms nominal -> gaps [1224, 1001, 1000, 1000, 1000, 999], mean 1037ms. 2000ms nominal -> ~3000ms gaps.
errorOne_throttleIsQuantizationNotAFacto.correctModel: Hidden-pane setTimeout is QUANTIZED TO 1-SECOND TICK BOUNDARIES: effective ~= ceil((nominal+eps)/1000)*1000. 250ms -> 1000ms. 900ms -> 1000ms. 2000ms -> 3000ms (a nominal exactly ON a boundary overshoots by eps and rounds UP a full second). This is the standard Chromium background-page timer clamp, not a proportional slowdown.
errorOne_throttleIsQuantizationNotAFacto.whyTheOldModelLookedRight: Poll 58 measured only at 2000ms nominal, where 2000 -> ~2822-3000ms reads as a plausible '1.41x'. Measuring at 250ms breaks the degeneracy immediately: no proportional factor turns 250ms into 1011ms. The old model was a curve fit through a single operating point.
errorOne_throttleIsQuantizationNotAFacto.itAlsoExplainsTheOldAnomaly: Poll 58's puzzling failure -- '12 samples x 1.9s = 20.9s nominal timed out despite being comfortably under 30s NOMINAL' -- falls straight out of quantization: 1900ms quantizes to 2000ms, so 11 sleeps cost 22000ms, not 20900ms. The multiplicative model predicted 29.5s and could not explain the death; quantization does.
errorOne_throttleIsQuantizationNotAFacto.resolutionIsBetterThanDocumented: The documented '~2s resolution' understates it -- the floor is 1s, so 1-second in-page sampling is achievable. But sub-second sampling is IMPOSSIBLE in a hidden pane at any nominal value, which the old model wrongly implied was available simply by shrinking the sleep.
errorOne_throttleIsQuantizationNotAFacto.practicalCorollary: Never request a sleep at an exact multiple of 1000ms; it sits on the knife edge and rounds up. Request just below a boundary (e.g. 900ms), which costs the same 1000ms but predictably.

errorTwo_the30sCapIsNotAnInPageBudget.observation: Three loops timed out this fire while shorter ones succeeded seconds apart with no throttle change: 8 samples x 1800ms with heavy per-sample work -> TIMEOUT; 19 x 900ms (~18s in-page) -> TIMEOUT; 14 x 900ms (~13s in-page) -> TIMEOUT. Meanwhile 6 x 900ms (~6s), 6 x 250ms (~6s) and 5 x 2000ms (14953ms measured in-page) all SUCCEEDED.
errorTwo_the30sCapIsNotAnInPageBudget.diagnosis: The 30s cap covers the WHOLE tool call, and round-trip/serialization overhead outside the page is both large and variable -- the state file already recorded '~18-60s observed' round trips. The usable in-page budget is 30s MINUS a variable 15-20s of overhead, i.e. roughly 6-10s, not 15s. The single 14953ms success was a low-overhead outlier, not proof that ~15s is safe.
errorTwo_the30sCapIsNotAnInPageBudget.throttleEscalationRuledOut: Explicitly tested, because Chromium applies INTENSIVE throttling (~1 timer/minute) to pages hidden >5 minutes, which would have been an alternative explanation. At 14:12:55-14:13:01, ~5.5 min into a hidden pane, gaps were still ~1000ms (mean 1037). No escalation. document.hidden === true and visibilityState === 'hidden' both confirmed, so the pane genuinely is a background page and the 1s clamp is the whole of the throttling observed today.
errorTwo_the30sCapIsNotAnInPageBudget.secondContributingCause: The 19-sample timeout ran across 14:11-14:12, exactly when the widget tore down the 19-row Red grid and built the 21-row Blue grid. Main-thread contention during a React grid swap plausibly delayed timers further. Not isolated from the overhead cause, but worth noting: in-page loops are LEAST reliable precisely during a session transition -- the moment they are most wanted.

CORRECTION_poll63.revisedDurableRule: Budget in-page loop wall time at <= ~8s per javascript_tool call (about 8 samples at the 1000ms quantization floor). Compute expected cost as ceil(nominal/1000)*1000 per sleep, never from nominal directly, and keep per-sample work minimal -- prefer parsing the flag carrier's inline style ATTRIBUTE over getComputedStyle across every descendant. For longer windows, chain short loops across successive tool calls. And ALWAYS put the state read BEFORE the sleep in each iteration so a timeout loses only the tail of the series: every timeout this fire returned nothing at all.
CORRECTION_poll63.methodNoteThatSavedThisFire: The ARM was ultimately caught not by a sampling loop but by a plain no-sleep probe, which has a 100% success rate today. When an event is imminent and the cadence is already short, prefer repeated cheap no-sleep probes over one clever loop.

CORRECTION_poll65.budgetRuleFailedAgain: The poll-63 revised rule ('budget in-page loop wall time at <= ~8s per call, about 8 samples at the 1000ms quantization floor') was followed EXACTLY -- 8 samples x 900ms nominal, ~8s in-page -- and still TIMED OUT, returning nothing. That is the documented budget, not an overrun of it. The usable budget is therefore variable fire-to-fire and cannot be expressed as a fixed number; overhead outside the page dominates and is not predictable in advance.
CORRECTION_poll65.revisedGuidance: Treat ANY sleeping in-page loop as unreliable. The no-sleep single probe has now succeeded on 100% of attempts across the whole day (dozens), while sleeping loops have failed repeatedly at every budget tried (44s, 21s, 18s, 13s, 8s). For event bracketing, issue repeated cheap no-sleep probes and accept the tool round-trip (~15-60s) as the resolution. This fire's Yellow->Finish transition was bracketed to 73s by exactly that approach, after the one sampling loop attempted cost ~30s and produced nothing.

busyWaitDefeatsTheClampButIsUSELESS.finding: A busy-wait spin (while(Date.now()-t<900){}) instead of setTimeout DOES defeat the hidden-pane 1-second timer clamp: measured inter-sample gaps were 900.0ms, 900.0ms, 900.0ms, 900.0ms, 900.0ms -- exactly nominal, zero quantization. So the poll-63 claim that 'sub-second sampling is IMPOSSIBLE in a hidden pane at any nominal value' is technically FALSE; it is impossible via setTimeout, not impossible per se.
busyWaitDefeatsTheClampButIsUSELESS.butItDoesNotHelP: It is nonetheless useless for the purpose. Busy-waiting blocks the main thread, so React cannot re-render and the DOM cannot update while you sample it. Across the entire 4.5s busy-wait window every single field was frozen -- flag, clock, ttg, ltg AND the widget's own wall clock all stuck at 14:38:57. Six samples returned six byte-identical readings of one instant.
busyWaitDefeatsTheClampButIsUSELESS.conclusion: Sub-second sampling and observing-change are mutually exclusive in this pane: setTimeout lets the page update but quantizes to 1s; busy-wait gives true sub-second cadence but starves the page of the updates being sampled. 1 second is the real floor for CHANGE DETECTION either way. Recorded so a future fire does not rediscover the busy-wait trick and mistake its precise-looking timestamps for a genuine resolution improvement -- the timestamps are real and the data behind them is stale, which is the dangerous combination.

CORRECTION_poll77.thisFiresData: 6 samples x 900ms: SUCCEEDED. 7 samples x 900ms: SUCCEEDED four times consecutively (16:10:51, 16:11:06, 16:11:21, 16:11:46). 8 samples x 900ms: TIMED OUT and returned nothing.
CORRECTION_poll77.relationToPriorCorrections: Poll 65 recorded 8x900ms failing and concluded 'treat ANY sleeping in-page loop as unreliable'. This fire shows 7x900ms succeeding four times in a row, so the loop is not uniformly unreliable -- but it also shows the failure boundary sitting at 8 samples again, exactly where poll 65 found it. The consistent reading across polls 58/63/65/77 is that the whole-call budget is ~30s, out-of-page overhead is variable and large, and roughly 6-7s of in-page time is what survives it on a good fire. None of that is predictable in advance.
CORRECTION_poll77.theActualLessonIsNotTheNUMBER: The number is a distraction. What this fire cost was the ONE measurement it most wanted: the 8-sample loop was scheduled deliberately across the predicted ttg->0 instant, it timed out, and the white-flag window (lapsToGo off the 9999 sentinel) passed unobserved inside the resulting 74s hole. Poll 58 recorded EXACTLY this failure -- 'two attempts to bracket the checkered with a tight in-page sampling loop both died on a tool timeout, costing the tightest measurement of the day at the exact moment it mattered' -- and it recurred verbatim.
CORRECTION_poll77.durableRuleEscalated: NEVER schedule a sleeping in-page loop across a PREDICTED event. A timeout returns nothing at all, so the loop converts the highest-value window of the fire into the only blind spot in it. Use sleeping loops ONLY to add resolution to an interval where nothing is expected, and cover predicted events with back-to-back no-sleep probes, which remain at a 100% success rate across the entire day. Cap any loop that is used at 6 samples.
CORRECTION_poll77.whatWorkedThisFire: The 1-second-resolution lap-flip capture at 16:10:19 came from a 6-sample loop run during a quiet interval -- the correct use of the technique. The checkered came from a no-sleep probe. Both halves of the rule are demonstrated within one fire.
