observedSessionsRecordHygiene.problem: observedSessions had accumulated DUPLICATE records for the same session -- two for Yellow Sprint 1 (widgetOrder 5) and two for Red Sprint 1 (widgetOrder 6). Each fire that learned something new about a session appended a fresh object instead of updating the existing one, so the array held two partial views of one session with silently divergent field values.
observedSessionsRecordHygiene.whyItMattered: A later reader doing sess[widgetOrder] or a first-match lookup would have gotten whichever record happened to come first -- for Red Sprint 1 that is the ARM-TIME record with greenAt:null and a 23-car arm-order class list including GT3/STG, not the post-session record with greenAt 13:08:07 and the 8-token running census. This is the same silent-wrong-answer family as the API's plausible-but-null field names: no error, just the wrong view.
observedSessionsRecordHygiene.fix: Merged to one record per session at poll 59. Divergent values are preserved under _mergeConflicts (not dropped) because several are real findings rather than corrections -- the arm-order grid genuinely contained classes that never took the green, and the arm row count genuinely differs from the running count.
observedSessionsRecordHygiene.goingForward: Update the existing record for a session in place; only append when widgetOrder is new.

apiSiblingCategoryStringIsStable.why: apiFinalResultsSelectionRule groups sibling records by (Name, CategoryString), while runGroupIdentificationByClassTokens proves CategoryString is a per-session CENSUS that shrinks when classes do not turn up. Those two facts look contradictory: if the string is unstable, how can it be a grouping key? This poll resolves the apparent conflict.
apiSiblingCategoryStringIsStable.finding: CategoryString varies BETWEEN sessions but is stable ACROSS the sibling records of ONE session, even when those siblings disagree on competitor count.

evidence.blueSprint1: Siblings 8720237 / 8720238 / 8720307 carry competitor counts 21 / 18 / 19 -- but all three publish the identical string '911CUP / E / GT4 / SP2 / SP3 / VGTO / VO / VU'.
evidence.yellowSprint1: Siblings 8720318 / 8720319 / 8720472 carry counts 29 / 28 / 28 -- all three publish the identical string 'G / I / J / ME1 / SPB / SPC'.
evidence.contrastWithBetweenSessionVariation: Across sessions the same run group DOES change string: the Blue Warm-Up drops E, the Yellow Warm-Up drops I, and the Red Warm-Up publishes only 3 of 11 Red tokens. Three-for-three, per runGroupIdentificationByClassTokens.

apiSiblingCategoryStringIsStable.interpretation: The census appears to be computed once per real on-track session and then copied verbatim onto every record published for it -- so it does NOT track the per-record competitor count. The 21-vs-18-vs-19 and 29-vs-28-vs-28 splits are a property of the snapshot each record froze, not of the class census.
apiSiblingCategoryStringIsStable.durableRule: (Name, CategoryString) is a valid key for grouping the sibling records OF ONE SESSION -- verified 2-for-2 on the only two sessions with complete sibling sets. It is NOT a valid key for identifying a run group ACROSS sessions, and string equality against a previously-seen CategoryString must never be used to ask 'has this run group's next session published yet?'. For that question, apply ANY-token membership against the three disjoint run-group universes after splitting the string on ' / '.
apiSiblingCategoryStringIsStable.limits: 2-for-2 is thin. Both confirmed cases are three-sibling groups from the same morning; neither Red Sprint 1 nor any Sprint 2 has published a sibling set to test against. A single counterexample -- one session whose siblings disagree on CategoryString -- would break the grouping key outright and force a fallback to (Name, run-group-universe). Re-test on the Sprint 2 sessions when they publish.
apiSiblingCategoryStringIsStable.relationToClaudeMdRules: Same seam as classTokenExtractionSiteTrap: one string is serving two different semantic roles (sibling identity vs run-group identity) and is only correct for one of them. The two roles need separate keys, not one string used twice.

redSprint1PublishPrediction.registered: 2026-08-08T14:04-04:00 (poll 62), BEFORE the record exists -- this is a pre-registered prediction, not a post-hoc reading.
redSprint1PublishPrediction.why: Red Sprint 1 is the first discriminating test of where CategoryString comes from. For Blue and Yellow Sprint 1 the ARM-order grid and the running census contained the same class tokens, so their published strings could not distinguish the two hypotheses. Red Sprint 1 differs: GT3 and STG were present in the armed grid but did NOT run (running census was GTB1/GTC3/GTC5/GTC6/GTC7/GTC8/GTD1/GTD2).
redSprint1PublishPrediction.hypothesisA_entryListDerived: Publishes as 'GT3 / GTB1 / GTC3 / GTC5 / GTC6 / GTC7 / GTC8 / GTD1 / GTD2 / STG' (10 tokens).
redSprint1PublishPrediction.hypothesisB_runningCensusDerived: Publishes as 'GTB1 / GTC3 / GTC5 / GTC6 / GTC7 / GTC8 / GTD1 / GTD2' (8 tokens).
redSprint1PublishPrediction.priorFavours: Hypothesis B, weakly. runGroupIdentificationByClassTokens found the Red Warm-Up published only 'GT3 / GTB1 / GTD2' -- 3 of 11 Red tokens for a 9-car field -- which looks census-shaped rather than entry-list-shaped. But that case is also not fully discriminating, since the warm-up's entry list may itself have been just those 3 classes.
redSprint1PublishPrediction.predictionThatHoldsEITHERWAY: Whichever branch is right, Red Sprint 1 will publish under a CategoryString that does NOT currently exist in the listing -- neither the 11-token practice/qualifying string nor the 3-token warm-up string. A consumer polling 'has the Red group's Sprint 1 published?' by string-equality against any previously-seen Red CategoryString will therefore return false FOREVER, even after the record lands. This is the concrete failure that apiSiblingCategoryStringIsStable.durableRule warns about, and Red Sprint 1 will be the first live instance of it.
redSprint1PublishPrediction.howToSettle: On the fire where Red Sprint 1 first appears, record the exact CategoryString and its token count, then mark hypothesis A or B.
redSprint1PublishPrediction.status: SETTLED 2026-08-08T14:28-04:00 (poll 64). HYPOTHESIS A -- ENTRY-LIST-DERIVED -- IS CORRECT.

resolution.publishedCategoryString: GT3 / GTB1 / GTC3 / GTC5 / GTC6 / GTC7 / GTC8 / GTD1 / GTD2 / STG -- 10 tokens.
resolution.verdict: Hypothesis A predicted exactly this 10-token string. Hypothesis B predicted the 8-token running census 'GTB1 / GTC3 / GTC5 / GTC6 / GTC7 / GTC8 / GTD1 / GTD2'. A wins; B is refuted.
resolution.mechanismNotJustTheOutcome: The Categories MAP on the record has 10 entries, and cross-referencing every competitor's Category id against it shows catIDs 2 (STG) and 6 (GT3) are referenced by ZERO of the 19 competitors. So the record carries two classes with no cars, and CategoryString is rendered from the Categories map rather than from the competitor set. That is the actual mechanism, and it is stronger evidence than the string alone -- it says WHY A is right, not merely that it matched.
resolution.priorWasWrong: The prediction recorded a weak prior for B, resting on the Red Warm-Up publishing only 3 of 11 Red tokens and on the Yellow Warm-Up (5 tokens) vs Yellow Sprint 1 (6 tokens) difference. Both are now explained by A without strain: those sessions simply had different ENTRY LISTS, not different running censuses. The census-shaped appearance was a coincidence of warm-ups being sparsely entered.
resolution.predictionThatHeldEitherWay_CONFIRMED: Red Sprint 1 did publish under a CategoryString that existed nowhere in the prior listing -- neither the 11-token practice/qualifying string (which includes GTD3) nor the 3-token warm-up string. A consumer polling by string-equality against previously-seen Red CategoryStrings would still be returning false. Confirmed live.
resolution.newDerivedCapability: Because Categories is a map and each competitor carries a Category id, the RUNNING CENSUS is recoverable from the API after all -- resolve the set of referenced ids through the map. Doing that on 8720598 yields exactly {GTB1,GTC3,GTC5,GTC6,GTC7,GTC8,GTD1,GTD2}, which matches the widget's .racerCategory census exactly. So the correct API method for 'which classes actually ran' is id-resolution, NEVER parsing CategoryString.

redSprint1PublishPrediction.durableRule: CategoryString is ENTRY-LIST-derived and over-reports: it lists classes that entered and did not run. Use it for run-group identification (it stays within one run-group universe, so the any-token-membership test is unaffected) but NEVER as 'which classes competed'. For that, resolve competitor Category ids through the Categories map. And never use CategoryString token COUNT as a field-size or participation proxy -- on Red Sprint 1 it overstates the competing-class count by 2 of 10.

apiProgressiveSnapshotChain.severity: MEDIUM-HIGH -- refines the core mental model of what API sibling records ARE, and exposes a gap in apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.
apiProgressiveSnapshotChain.trigger: Enumerating (Name, CategoryString) groups across all 29 sessions turned up a FIVE-member sibling group -- 'Practice 1 | GT3 / GTB1 / GTC3 / GTC5 / GTC6 / GTC7 / GTC8 / GTD1 / GTD2 / GTD3 / STG' -- above the 2-3 maximum documented in apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.

data.fetchHygiene: all five fetched individually; each HTTP 200, application/json, non-empty body, .Successful true, .Session.SortedCompetitors non-empty (cardinality asserted per apiSessionDetailsSchemaTrap.reWalkedAtPoll54)

apiProgressiveSnapshotChain.finding: ID order, epoch order, competitor count and maxLaps all rise essentially monotonically together. These are not a stub plus a final -- they are a CHAIN OF PROGRESSIVE MID-SESSION SNAPSHOTS, each frozen when written, each published under its own new session ID, spanning ~10 minutes of wall time (615s first-to-last epoch).
apiProgressiveSnapshotChain.howThisRevisesThePriorModel: apiInProgressSnapshotFrozen and apiDualPublish framed the pattern as a small number of frozen stubs plus a real final landing later under a new ID. The correct generalisation: the API emits a stream of frozen snapshots per session, of arbitrary length (>=5 observed), and the 'real final' is simply the last snapshot IF the session was ever finalised. Stub-vs-final is not a type distinction between two kinds of record; it is a position-in-chain distinction, and completeness is a property only of the chain's tail.

theGapThisOpensInTheSelectionRule.problem: apiFinalResultsSelectionRule pairs highest-ID-within-(Name, CategoryString) with a maxLaps plausibility check and treats a failed check as 'not ready yet, keep polling'. For Practice 1 Red the highest ID (8718696) has maxLaps 10, which for a practice session of unknown configured length may itself be a mid-session snapshot rather than a final.
theGapThisOpensInTheSelectionRule.consequence: The plausibility check cannot distinguish 'not finalised YET' from 'never finalised AT ALL'. Both present as an implausible tail. A consumer polling for Practice 1 Red's final would poll forever, and per apiNoProvisionalFlag there is no field marking a record provisional to break the tie. Same structural defect as Red Sprint 1's indefinite absence, one level down: absence and incompleteness are both indistinguishable from lateness.
theGapThisOpensInTheSelectionRule.mitigation: Any ingestion consumer needs a TIMEOUT with an explicit typed outcome -- 'no final published within N minutes of the widget-observed teardown' must be recorded as its own state (unresolved/abandoned), never as a still-pending poll and never as an empty session. Per the CLAUDE.md No-Log-Scraping rule this is a typed branch, not something to infer from how the payload happens to look.

apiProgressiveSnapshotChain.epochOrderingCaveat: In THIS group the five epochs are distinct and their order agrees with ID order, so epoch would have selected correctly here. That does not rehabilitate epoch: it still fails on the documented exact-epoch ties (Blue Sprint 1's 8720238/8720307 both 1786200139; Practice 3 Red's 8718867/8718885 both 1786129177) and it still is not publication time (apiFinalResultsSelectionRule.epochIsNotPublishTime). Highest-ID remains the selection key; this group is simply a case where the two agree.
apiProgressiveSnapshotChain.openQuestion: Unknown whether chain length correlates with anything useful (session length, red flags, timing-system restarts). Practice 1 Red has 5; Practice 3 Blue, Practice 3 Red and both Sprint 1 groups have 3; most sessions have 1. Worth tabulating chain length against known session incidents on a future capture day.

poll64_blueSprint2LiveChain.observation: Blue Sprint 2, still green, already has TWO sibling records: 8720631 (epoc 1786212666 = 14:11:06, 21 competitors, maxLaps 8) and 8720632 (epoc 1786213652 = 14:27:32, 20 competitors, maxLaps 8). Caught mid-session rather than reconstructed afterwards, which is new.
poll64_blueSprint2LiveChain.epocIsNotSessionStartForLaterSiblings: This is the cleanest disproof yet of reading SessionStartDateEpoc as a session-start time. 8720631's epoc 14:11:06 falls INSIDE the independently-bracketed ARM window (14:09:58 -> 14:11:13) -- so the first sibling's epoc is arm-shaped. But 8720632's epoc is 14:27:32, roughly one minute before the poll that first saw it and 16 minutes after the session started. The field therefore ADVANCES with each snapshot; it is closer to a snapshot-creation time than to a session start, and it is not consistent between siblings of one session. Combined with the already-recorded exact-epoch TIE on Blue Sprint 1 (8720238 and 8720307 both 1786200139), SessionStartDateEpoc is now disqualified as a key for recency, for stub-vs-final discrimination, AND for session-start timing. It should be treated as opaque.
poll64_blueSprint2LiveChain.maxLapsIsStaleWhileLive: Both stubs report maxLaps 8 while the widget leader is on 10 laps at the same instant. Consistent with apiInProgressSnapshotFrozen: the snapshot is written once and not updated, so a live consumer reading maxLaps trails the truth by minutes.
poll64_blueSprint2LiveChain.lastLapTimeIsNearlyEmptyInSnapshots: NEW: in 8720632, LastLapTime is the EMPTY STRING for 19 of 20 competitors -- only #753 carries a value -- while the widget renders a well-formed Last Time for every one of its 20 rows at the same moment. BestLapTime and TotalTime ARE populated for the same competitors, so this is not a wholesale blank record. Any consumer treating LastLapTime as reliably present will see near-total loss on mid-session snapshots. Adds a concrete field-level instance to the general widgetLeadsApiForFinalResults finding.

poll65_minimalDeltaBetweenSiblings.why: Poll 64 established that Blue Sprint 2's two live siblings existed and were both stale. This fire DIFFED them field-by-field, which pins the snapshot-chain model far more tightly than a count comparison can.
poll65_minimalDeltaBetweenSiblings.delta: Across 21 vs 20 competitors, 8720631 -> 8720632 differ in EXACTLY two ways: (1) #753 DAVID DEAN Laps '7'->'8' and TotalTime 00:11:14.551->00:12:51.764; (2) #271 (Position '21', Laps '', BestLapTime 00:00:00.000, TotalTime 00:00:00.000) is PRUNED. All other 19 competitors are byte-identical on Position/Laps/BestLapTime/TotalTime.
poll65_minimalDeltaBetweenSiblings.whatThisProves: The siblings are genuinely PROGRESSIVE snapshots of one session, not independent re-derivations and not stub-vs-final: the later one is the earlier one plus a single car's completed lap, minus a non-starter. A one-lap delta across a 16m26s epoc gap also shows the epoc spacing does NOT correspond to the snapshot content's time spacing -- another nail in SessionStartDateEpoc as any kind of clock.
poll65_minimalDeltaBetweenSiblings.nonStarterPruningIsNewBehaviour: #271 appears in the earlier sibling with an empty Laps and a zeroed BestLapTime, then vanishes from the later one. So the API DOES eventually drop never-ran entries -- but only on a later snapshot, and an ingestion consumer reading the earlier sibling would record a 21-car field for a race 20 cars started. Combined with the already-documented apiBlankNumericFields, the rule for consumers is: a competitor with Laps=='' is a non-starter placeholder and must not be counted in field size, REGARDLESS of which sibling it came from -- do not rely on the API to have pruned it.
poll65_minimalDeltaBetweenSiblings.relationToCategoryString: Consistent with redSprint1PublishPrediction's settled hypothesis A: the record is rendered from the ENTRY LIST, so entered-but-never-ran competitors and classes are present until something prunes them. #271 is the competitor-level instance of exactly the mechanism GT3/STG showed at the class level.

COMPLETE_CHAIN_poll78.significance: First time all three records of one session's chain were visible in the same listing and fetched in the same fire, so the chain is documented end to end rather than reconstructed across fires.

records.role: 20-row POST-CULL stub, still frozen at lap 2

COMPLETE_CHAIN_poll78.duplicateEpochSiblings: 8720921 and 8721056 carry the IDENTICAL SessionStartDateEpoc 1786218419. This is the sharpest instance of the duplicate-epoch hazard seen today: a max-by-epoch selector ties between a 2-lap frozen stub and the 20-lap real result and breaks the tie on whatever order the JSON happens to arrive in. Max-by-ID resolved it correctly here, but max-by-ID is not independently validated as the rule -- it is merely consistent with every case observed today.
COMPLETE_CHAIN_poll78.cullIsAPublishNotAnEdit: The 29 -> 20 field cull appears as a SEPARATE RECORD (8720920 vs 8720921), not as a mutation of the first. Records in this API appear to be immutable once written; progress is expressed by publishing a new sibling. That is why the stubs never 'catch up'.
COMPLETE_CHAIN_poll78.publishLag: Checkered <= 16:13:06; 8721056 complete and fetchable by ~16:22:15. Upper bound 9m09s.
COMPLETE_CHAIN_poll78.widgetAgreement: 8721056's top three match the widget's 16:13:22 final grid exactly, best-lap times to the millisecond. The API is late, but on this session it was not wrong.
COMPLETE_CHAIN_poll78.durableRule: Select final results by (Name, CategoryString) grouping and then MAX ID, never max epoch, and never trust a single record's lap counts without checking whether a higher-ID sibling with the same epoch exists.

sessionNameChangeIsASignalButOnlySometim.observation: The arm of Blue Sprint 2 produced the FIRST session-name change of the day: the header field went from 'Sprint 1\r' to 'Sprint 2\r'. Every poll from 10:38 through 14:09:58 read 'Sprint 1', across three different run groups and three separate sessions, because all three were named 'Sprint 1'.
sessionNameChangeIsASignalButOnlySometim.whyItMatters: For this one arm the name change is the single most legible ARM signal in the header -- more obvious than the lapsToGo sentinel. It is tempting to promote it into the ARM signature. That would be a mistake.
sessionNameChangeIsASignalButOnlySometim.whyItIsNotAReliableArmSignal: The name identifies the SESSION TYPE, not the run group (sessionNameDoesNotIdentifyRunGroup) and not the session instance. Today it was constant across the Blue -> Yellow -> Red Sprint 1 rotation, so it changed on 1 of 4 observed arms. It changes only when consecutive sessions happen to carry different names, which is a property of the event schedule, not of the state machine. Concretely: the upcoming Yellow Sprint 2 and Red Sprint 2 arms will BOTH read 'Sprint 2' following this session, so the name will be static across both -- exactly as it was static across the three Sprint 1 arms.
sessionNameChangeIsASignalButOnlySometim.durableRule: Treat the session name as a LABEL to record and to help a human disambiguate, never as an edge-trigger. A name change implies a new session; an unchanged name implies nothing at all. Same asymmetry as the leaderboard: mutation is informative, stasis is not (leaderboardPersistsThroughTeardown, elemCountIsNotAChangeDetector). Retain lapsToGo 0 -> 9999 plus grid freshness as the ARM trigger.
sessionNameChangeIsASignalButOnlySometim.alsoConfirms: sessionNameTrailingCarriageReturn -- 'Sprint 2\r' carries the same trailing CR as 'Sprint 1\r'.

fieldShrinkIsRealAndApiVisible.observation: The Blue Sprint 2 widget leaderboard went from 21 rows at ARM (14:11:13) to 20 rows now, with maxPos also 20 -- so this is a genuine row removal, not a selector artifact, and the independent maxPos witness agrees per substringClassSelectorDoubleCount.correctSelector.
fieldShrinkIsRealAndApiVisible.mechanismIdentifiedFromTheApi: The two Blue Sprint 2 snapshots isolate the missing car exactly. 8720631 (21 competitors) contains #271 PATTI MASCONE with Laps='' and LastLapTime=''; 8720632 (20 competitors) does not contain her at all. So a car that never completed a lap is carried briefly with a BLANK Laps string and is then dropped from both the API record and the widget board.
fieldShrinkIsRealAndApiVisible.whyThisMatters: It gives the mechanism behind leaderboardRowCountIsNotFieldSize and behind Red Sprint 1's '24 rows at ARM -> 19 running rows' churn, which was previously only described. Entered-but-non-starting cars are provisionally on the board, then removed. Row count is therefore a decreasing function of time early in a session and stabilises only once every non-starter has been culled.
fieldShrinkIsRealAndApiVisible.blankIsNotZero: #271's Laps is the empty string, NOT '0'. apiBlankNumericFields already warns about this class of value; this is a live instance in a field a consumer would naturally treat as an integer, and it is the SPECIFIC value that broke this fire's own tooling -- see jqParseErrorMisdirection.
fieldShrinkIsRealAndApiVisible.durableRule: Never treat a drop in leaderboard row count as an error, a scrape failure, or a session change. Early-session shrinkage is normal and expected. Conversely, never latch field size from the armed grid: take it after the count has been stable across at least two polls.

jqParseErrorMisdirection.severity: MEDIUM-HIGH -- it produced a WRONG DIAGNOSIS that was one step from being written into this file as a confirmed finding.
jqParseErrorMisdirection.whatHappened: Parsing 8720631 with jq emitted: `jq: error (at sd631_1.json:0): Expected JSON value (while parsing '')`. Every surface signal agreed with a transport/body fault: offset 0, the phrase 'Expected JSON value', and an empty-string literal. The reflex reading was 'empty or truncated body' -- i.e. a reproduction of the existing apiTransientEmptyBody finding.
jqParseErrorMisdirection.whatWasActuallyTrue: The body was completely fine: HTTP 200, Content-Type application/json, 7961 bytes, first bytes `{"Successful":true,...`, last bytes `...1786212666}}`, and Python's json.loads parsed it without complaint. The real fault was inside the jq PROGRAM: `.Laps|tonumber` was applied to #271 PATTI MASCONE's blank Laps field. jq reports that as a parse error attributed to the INPUT FILE at offset 0.
jqParseErrorMisdirection.howItWasCaught: Only by refusing to accept the message and checking independently -- hexdumping both ends of the file and re-parsing with a different JSON implementation. Python's error, `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: ''`, names the actual fault immediately. Three curl retries had already 'confirmed' the failure was reproducible, which made the wrong diagnosis look stronger, not weaker: the bug reproduced perfectly because it was deterministic and had nothing to do with the network.
jqParseErrorMisdirection.relationToClaudeMdRules: Direct instance of the No-Log-Scraping / structured-signalling rule. A free-text error string was about to be used to classify a fault, and its text pointed at the wrong subsystem entirely -- transport instead of data content. The rule's premise holds exactly: this misdirection arrives at the moment of failure, when there is least room for a wrong branch. A consumer that retried-on-'parse error' would have hammered the endpoint forever against a body that was never going to change.
jqParseErrorMisdirection.durableRule: Do not classify a JSON failure from the parser's message. Validate the body independently -- length, first/last bytes, Content-Type -- before concluding anything about transport, and re-parse with a second implementation before blaming the payload. Concretely for jq: `tonumber` on a blank string surfaces as an input-parse error at offset 0, so guard every numeric coercion over API data as `[.Session.SortedCompetitors[].Laps | select(. != "") | tonumber]`. This applies to EVERY numeric field on this API, since apiFieldTypesAreStrings means they are all strings and any of them can be blank.
jqParseErrorMisdirection.verification: Same bytes, three tools: jq -> misleading input-parse error at offset 0; python json.loads -> parses, then fails at the int() with the true cause named; xxd -> well-formed JSON at both ends. The disagreement is entirely in the error reporting, not in the data.

widgetCanRenderABlankClassToken.observation: #711 ROBERT BRANTHOVER's row renders an EMPTY .racerCategory in the widget. Verified structurally, not by eye: a scan of all 20 .racerCategory nodes found exactly one blank, it IS inside a .racerRowStacked row, and its sibling text is '#711 ROBERT BRANTHOVER'.
widgetCanRenderABlankClassToken.theApiDisagrees: In 8720632 the same car carries Category id 3, which the Categories map resolves to 'SP3' -- a perfectly ordinary Blue-universe class. So the class is known to the timing system and simply is not rendered in this widget row. His AdditionalData is also empty in the API, while other cars carry livery/model strings, so the row is sparsely populated generally.
widgetCanRenderABlankClassToken.consequenceForTheStopCondition: classTokenExtractionSiteTrap makes .racerCategory the sole legitimate extraction site for run-group identification, and that stands. But the extracted SET can now contain the empty string, and an individual row can contribute NO token at all. Two failure modes follow: an extractor that asserts every row yields a token will throw on a legitimate page, and one that adds '' to the universe will find '' in no run-group universe and may report an unknown or mixed group.
widgetCanRenderABlankClassToken.durableRule: Filter blank tokens out of the .racerCategory set BEFORE the any-token-membership test, and assert only that the resulting set is non-empty and lands in exactly one universe -- never that every row contributed. If the widget class is needed for a specific car rather than for group identification, fall back to resolving the API's Category id through the Categories map, which was populated for this car when the widget was not.
widgetCanRenderABlankClassToken.relationToPriorFindings: Third distinct defect found in the same run-group extraction path, after classTokenExtractionSiteTrap (wrong site) and substringClassSelectorDoubleCount (wrong selector). The path keeps producing them, which reinforces that finding's suggestion of one canonical row-and-field accessor consumed by every probe rather than per-poll selectors.

poll81_SECOND_INSTANCE_AND_IT_IS_A_MUTAT.whatItChangesAboutThisEntry: This entry's framing -- 'the class is known to the timing system and simply is not rendered in this widget row', with the supporting note that the car's row is 'sparsely populated generally' -- reads as a STATIC per-car data gap. That is falsified. The same widget rendered 'GTC5' for #51 at 16:22:40 on this session's ARMED grid and blank from 16:41:39 onward. The cell changed mid-session, on a car that is still circulating normally (lap 15, last 01:26.939, best 01:25.898 -- every other cell populated).
poll81_SECOND_INSTANCE_AND_IT_IS_A_MUTAT.sparsenessDoesNotExplainIt: Unlike #711, #51 is NOT sparsely populated. His .additionalData, .lapsValue, .lastTimeValue, .bestLapValue, .bestTimeValue, .diffValue and .gapValue are all present and current, and the API gives him a livery ('WHITE'). poll81_SECOND_INSTANCE_AND_IT_IS_A_MUTAT.theDurableRuleHELD: This entry's prescribed fallback -- resolve the class through the API's Categories map -- was executed and WORKED: .Session.Categories['7'].Name resolves #51's Category id 7 to 'GTC5', matching what the widget itself displayed 22 minutes earlier. First confirmation of the rule on a car other than the one that produced it.
poll81_SECOND_INSTANCE_AND_IT_IS_A_MUTAT.escalation: The consequence is larger than this entry recorded. Because #51 is the group's only GTC5 entrant, his blank cell removes GTC5 from the widget's class census ENTIRELY -- the universe shrank from ten tokens to nine mid-session. See widgetClassCensusCanLoseAnEntireToken.
poll81_SECOND_INSTANCE_AND_IT_IS_A_MUTAT.instanceCount: Two cars, two run groups, one confirmed mid-session mutation. Frequency is now high enough that a consumer must handle it as normal operation rather than as an anomaly.

poll83_RESOLVED_BY_API_CROSS_REFERENCE.resolution: The blank .racerCategory belongs to #51 ROBERT HARGESHEIMER at P18. poll83_RESOLVED_BY_API_CROSS_REFERENCE.whyTheWholeTokenVanishesFromTheCensus: The per-category census for this session is {GTC8:1, STG:1, GTC7:1, GTC3:3, GTD1:1, GT3:2, GTC5:1, GTD2:1, GTC6:1, GTB1:10}. poll83_RESOLVED_BY_API_CROSS_REFERENCE.independentCorroboration: The session-level CategoryString is 'GT3 / GTB1 / GTC3 / GTC5 / GTC6 / GTC7 / GTC8 / GTD1 / GTD2 / STG' = 10 tokens. poll83_RESOLVED_BY_API_CROSS_REFERENCE.severityForCameraControl: A single-entry class is precisely the case where a per-class camera rule would silently never fire. The failure is invisible: 22 rows render, 21 have classes, nothing errors.

yellowFlagState.significance: FIRST CAUTION OF THE DAY, after 8 sessions and 64 prior polls. Extends the observed flag vocabulary from {Green, Finish, ''} to {Green, Yellow, Finish, ''} and is the first flag state that is neither a session start nor a session end -- i.e. the first one an automated camera controller would have to react to MID-session.

signature.styleAttr: top: 7px; right: 40px; font-weight: bold; text-align: right; color: rgb(255, 255, 0);
signature.verdict: IDENTICAL carrier signature to Green and Finish on every structural axis -- same sole-bold-child discriminator, same index, same style-attribute shape, only the text and the color hex differ. The flagCarrierSignature extractor needed ZERO changes to read it. This is the strongest possible validation of that signature: it generalised to a state it had never seen.

yellowFlagState.colorTextAgreement: Text and color AGREE here (Yellow/rgb(255,255,0)), unlike the idle state where text is empty and the color is stale-retained. So the text/color DISAGREEMENT remains diagnostic of idle specifically, not a general property of the carrier.

observedWindow.note: true duration longer at both ends -- see onsetBracket; it ended by becoming the Finish, not by returning to Green

onsetBracket.rawBracketWidth: 7m36s (prior fire's last probe was Green at 14:30:16)

yellowFlagState.clockBehaviourUnderCaution: The session clock and time-to-go RUN NORMALLY under yellow. Green re-derived as EXACTLY 14:14:41 at 14:37:52 (clock 00:23:11) and again at 14:40:57 (clock 00:26:16) -- zero drift across the entire caution, 26m37s total. clock+ttg held at the configured 00:29:59 throughout the yellow as well. A caution therefore costs the session real time; it does not pause it. Directly relevant to shot planning: time-to-go remains a valid wall-clock countdown during a caution.
yellowFlagState.lapsToGoUnderCaution: Held the 9999 sentinel for the entire caution. Yellow does NOT perturb lapsToGo.
yellowFlagState.leaderboardCorroboration: INDEPENDENT second signal, and a strong one: at 14:38:17 ALL 20 cars showed Last Time between 01:47.830 and 03:45.637 against personal bests of 01:24.673-01:46.144 -- a field-wide simultaneous ~30-90s inflation. Leader #66 ran 01:57.773 (lap 15, caught the yellow mid-lap) then 02:54.458 (lap 16, full caution lap) against a 01:24.673 best. No plausible mechanism other than a full-course caution produces synchronised inflation across an entire field.
yellowFlagState.whyTheCorroborationMatters: It gives a SECOND, structurally independent detector for caution -- median-last-lap-vs-median-best ratio across the field -- that does not depend on the flag carrier's DOM at all. For camera control this is worth implementing as a cross-check: if the carrier says Green but the whole field is running 1.5-2x its best pace, one of the two signals is wrong and the system should degrade safely rather than trust either blindly. Note the ratio lags the flag by up to one lap (a car only reports the slow lap once it completes it), so it confirms rather than predicts.
openQuestions: Never observed a Yellow -> Green RESTART today (this caution ran straight into the Finish). The restart transition, and whether any distinct intermediate state exists, is completely unobserved.
Unknown whether local/regional yellows render differently from a full-course yellow, or at all.
Unknown whether a RED flag uses the same carrier (presumably text 'Red', rgb(255,0,0)) -- never observed.
Unknown whether the carrier can show any other vocabulary (Black, White, Checkered as distinct from 'Finish', Meatball).

RESOLVED-AS-POSSIBLE at poll 66: Finish -> Yellow reversion DOES occur (post-checkered, during the hold). Still open: whether this yellow clears back to Finish, to blank, or runs straight into teardown.

poll66_secondYellowSameSession.what: A SECOND yellow within Blue Sprint 2, this one AFTER the checkered, reached by a Finish -> Yellow reversion rather than a Green -> Yellow onset. Carrier text/color literals byte-identical to the 14:37:52 caution.
poll66_secondYellowSameSession.colorTextAgreementHolds: Text 'Yellow' and color rgb(255,255,0) agree, as at the first caution. The text/color DISAGREEMENT remains diagnostic of idle only.
poll66_secondYellowSameSession.corroborationUnavailableHere: The leaderboard cross-check that corroborated the first caution (field-wide lap-time inflation) CANNOT corroborate this one: lap counts are frozen post-checkered, so no new lap times are being posted to inflate. The independent second detector described in whyTheCorroborationMatters is therefore unavailable exactly in the post-checkered window -- worth knowing before relying on it as a general safety cross-check.
poll66_secondYellowSameSession.answersOneOpenQuestion: The openQuestions list asked only about Yellow -> Green restarts and about other vocabulary. It did not consider that Finish -> Yellow was possible at all. Added there now.

poll79_FIRST_RESTART_RED_SPRINT_2.significance: SECOND caution of the day and the FIRST that ended in a RESTART rather than in the Finish. This closes openQuestions[0], which had stood since poll 65.
poll79_FIRST_RESTART_RED_SPRINT_2.carrierBehaviour: Yellow -> Green directly, no intermediate value observed at 58s resolution. Carrier signature needed zero changes for a third consecutive flag state; the sole-bold-child discriminator has now read Green, Yellow, Finish and idle-empty without modification.
poll79_FIRST_RESTART_RED_SPRINT_2.clockDidNotPause: The decisive measurement. Green re-derives as EXACTLY 16:22:58 at 16:28:49 and 16:29:13 (both under yellow), at 16:30:11 (the restart probe itself), and at 16:30:36 / 16:31:06 / 16:31:49 / 16:32:18 (all after). Zero drift across the entire caution AND the restart. clock+ttg held 00:29:59 throughout. This extends clockBehaviourUnderCaution, which was measured on a caution that ran straight into the Finish, to the restart case -- a caution costs the session real time and a restart does not credit any back.
poll79_FIRST_RESTART_RED_SPRINT_2.consequenceForCameraControl: A restart is a high-value shot moment (field bunched, green-flag racing resumes at a known instant) and the feed DOES signal it -- but only coincidently, in the same carrier, with no lead time whatsoever. There is no armed/pending-restart state in this feed. A controller wanting to be pre-positioned for a restart cannot get advance warning from RaceMonitor and must either hold finish-posture for the duration of every caution or accept reacting ~1 poll late.
openQuestionsNowRemaining: Whether an intermediate carrier state exists inside the 58s restart bracket (needs a fire that catches a restart at ~1s probe cadence).
Whether a RED flag uses the same carrier (presumably 'Red' / rgb(255,0,0)) -- still never observed.
Whether local vs full-course yellows render differently -- still unknown, and this fire cannot distinguish them because both of today's cautions were read only through the carrier.
Black / White / Meatball / Checkered-distinct-from-Finish vocabulary -- still unobserved.

cautionOnsetReconstructionFromLapTimes.problem: Polling cadence is ~5-8 minutes, but a caution's onset needs finer resolution than that to be useful as a training/label signal for camera control. The raw poll bracket for this caution was 7m36s wide.
cautionOnsetReconstructionFromLapTimes.method: Use the leader's per-lap times as a much finer clock than the poll interval. A full-caution lap and a green lap differ by ~2x, and a lap that STRADDLES the onset lands in between. Work backwards from a known-time anchor: leader's lap 16 (02:54.458, fully-caution-shaped) ended at the Finish (bracketed 14:39:44-14:40:57), so lap 16 began ~14:38:03, so lap 15 (01:57.773) began ~14:36:05. Lap 15 is intermediate between a 01:26 green lap and a 02:54 caution lap, so the yellow fell DURING lap 15 -- i.e. between 14:36:05 and its completion, and it was already flying at the 14:37:52 observation.
cautionOnsetReconstructionFromLapTimes.result: Narrowed the onset from a 7m36s poll bracket to ~1m47s (14:36:05-14:37:52), a >4x improvement, using data already captured rather than any extra polling.
assumptions: leader's green-lap pace ~01:26 (his last green lap was 01:26.841, best 01:24.673)
lap 15's inflation is attributable to the caution and not to traffic or an off
the Finish instant is within its observed bracket
cautionOnsetReconstructionFromLapTimes.selfConsistencyCheck: The reconstruction independently predicts lap 15 completing ~14:38:03; the widget showed the leader's completed-lap count reaching 15 by 14:37:52. Agreement within ~11s, comfortably inside the widget's own update lag. The chain is internally consistent, which is the main reason to trust it.
cautionOnsetReconstructionFromLapTimes.caveat: This is INFERENCE, not observation, and it is recorded as such. It is only as good as the assumed green-lap pace. It should never be written into a flagTransitions entry as if directly observed -- the raw poll bracket is retained alongside it above.
cautionOnsetReconstructionFromLapTimes.generalisation: Any field-wide pace discontinuity can be back-solved this way for any flag event whose end is anchored to an observed instant. Worth applying retrospectively if a future capture day needs finer caution labels than its poll cadence delivered.

finishIsNotTerminal.significance: Overturns an assumption this state file has carried implicitly all day: that within one session the flag carrier progresses monotonically to Finish and stays there until teardown. It does not. Blue Sprint 2 read Finish/white from 14:40:57 through 14:44:58 and then read Yellow/rgb(255,255,0) from 14:47:39 through at least 14:49:03, with no intervening teardown.

sameSessionProof.clock: Advanced continuously and re-derived green as EXACTLY 14:14:41 at all three post-reversion probes -- identical to the derivation at 14:37:52, 14:40:57 and 14:44:58. A new session would have restarted the clock at 00:00:00.
sameSessionProof.lapsToGo: Held the 9999 sentinel throughout. The confirmed teardown signal (9999 -> 0) never fired.
sameSessionProof.sessionName: Still 'Sprint 2'; unchanged (though see sessionNameDoesNotIdentifyRunGroup -- this axis is weak evidence on its own).
sameSessionProof.grid: 20 rows, every Laps value byte-identical to the 14:41:18 final classification (#66 on 16, #43 on 16, #15 on 15, ... #08 on 9). Only LastTime fields have moved, all now ~02:5x, i.e. cool-down in-laps.

finishIsNotTerminal.mostLikelyMechanism: The carrier reports TRACK condition, not SESSION lifecycle state. After the checkered the cars are still circulating on their in-laps while corner workers and recovery vehicles go out -- plausibly to retrieve whatever caused the 14:36 caution that ended this session early. The tower puts the track back under yellow for that, and the widget faithfully mirrors it. This reading is CONSISTENT with everything observed but is NOT directly verified -- no independent confirmation of on-track activity is available from the feed.
finishIsNotTerminal.whyTheAlternativesAreWeaker: (a) 'A new session armed' is refuted by the continuous clock and the retained 16-lap grid. (b) 'A rendering glitch' is weak: the state held across three probes spanning 1m24s with a byte-identical style attribute, and the yellow is the exact same literal as the earlier validated caution. (c) 'The hold ended and a fresh yellow belongs to the NEXT session' is refuted by lapsToGo never leaving 9999 and by the grid still carrying Blue Sprint 2's results.
finishIsNotTerminal.cameraControlImplication: HIGH. Two concrete consequences. (1) A controller that treats Finish as a latching end-of-session marker -- e.g. one that stops polling, tears down state, or arms a 'wait for next session' branch on first sight of Finish -- will be caught out by the flag going back to Yellow while the same session is still displayed. Finish must be modelled as a transient track condition, and END-OF-SESSION must key on the already-validated teardown signal (lapsToGo 9999 -> 0 AND clock -> 00:00:00), NOT on the Finish flag. This is the third independent argument for that same rule, alongside postCheckeredHoldState.stopConditionImplication and leaderboardMutatesDuringHold. (2) A yellow during the hold is genuinely actionable for a camera: it means recovery equipment is on track and cars are circulating slowly -- different shot planning from either racing or a torn-down idle.
finishIsNotTerminal.detectorConsequence: The state machine documented in this task's own prompt (IDLE -> ARMED -> GREEN -> FINISH -> IDLE) is a DAG and is now known to be wrong. The GREEN/YELLOW/FINISH states form a cycle: any of them can follow any other while lapsToGo == 9999. The only edges that are actually reliable are the two lapsToGo transitions -- 0 -> 9999 (arm) and 9999 -> 0 (teardown). A correct implementation should treat lapsToGo as the session-lifecycle variable and the flag carrier as an INDEPENDENT track-condition variable, not as two views of one state machine.
openQuestions: Does this yellow clear back to Finish, to blank, or straight to teardown? Unobserved as of 14:49:03 -- watch on the next fire.

Does the same reversion happen after a NORMAL (non-caution-shortened) finish, or is it specific to a session that ended under caution with something still on track? Two full-distance finishes remain today (Yellow Sprint 2, Red Sprint 2) to test this.

Did any earlier hold today do this and get missed? Plausible -- prior holds were sampled at ~3-5 min intervals and this reversion appeared between the 4m01s and 6m42s marks. The Red Warm-Up, Blue Sprint 1, Yellow Sprint 1 and Red Sprint 1 holds all have gaps wide enough to have hidden one. This is an argument that the day's earlier hold characterisations are UNDER-sampled, not that they were wrong.
finishIsNotTerminal.relationToPriorFindings: Directly extends yellowFlagState, whose openQuestions listed 'never observed a Yellow -> Green RESTART'. Still true -- but the flag vocabulary's TRANSITION graph turns out to be richer than the vocabulary itself suggested, and the unobserved-transition list should have included Finish -> Yellow. Also a fourth validation of flagCarrierSignature: the extractor read a transition it was never designed for with zero changes.

poll68_SECOND_YELLOW_EPISODE.what: The carrier read 'Yellow'/rgb(255,255,0) again, having held 'Finish' from the 14:52:24 reversion through the 14:58:34 probe. Flag edge sequence for this single session's hold is now: Finish (14:40:57) -> Yellow (<=14:52:09) -> Finish (14:52:24) -> Yellow (<=15:03:31). Three edges, two Yellow episodes, in under 24 minutes.
poll68_SECOND_YELLOW_EPISODE.whyThisMattersMoreThanTheFirstOscillatio: One Finish->Yellow reversion could be dismissed as a single post-race stewards' action or a one-off publisher glitch. A SECOND, several minutes later and after an intervening return to Finish, establishes that the flag field during the hold is a repeatedly-mutating scratch value, not a state that settles. Any consumer that treats the first 'Finish' as latching, or that debounces flag changes over a few minutes and then latches, will still be wrong here.
poll68_SECOND_YELLOW_EPISODE.detectorConsequence: REINFORCES AND HARDENS the existing rule. 'Finish' must never latch a controller into an end-of-session state, and no debounce window short of the full teardown is safe -- the quiet intervals between these edges were ~11min and ~6min, longer than any plausible debounce. Only the lapsToGo 9999 -> 0 teardown edge may be treated as terminal. Restated as a bound: on today's evidence the flag carrier is NOT a monotone function of session progress after the checkered, so it cannot be consumed as a state machine input during the hold at all -- only as an observation to log.
poll68_SECOND_YELLOW_EPISODE.cameraControlImplication: A controller that resumed shooting on a Yellow after the checkered would fire twice here, ~11 minutes apart, on a session that has been over for 20+ minutes. The teardown gate is doing all the real work; the flag is doing none of it during the hold.
poll68_SECOND_YELLOW_EPISODE.openQuestion: Whether these post-checkered Yellow episodes are correlated with the leaderboard replay stepping (both moved in the same 4m57s bracket this fire, and both moved together in the 14:52 bracket too). Two co-occurrences is suggestive, not causal. A third co-occurrence -- or a leaderboard step WITHOUT a flag edge -- would discriminate. Watch for it explicitly next fire.

poll69.fourthEdge: Yellow -> Finish, bracketed 15:04:39 < t <= 15:12:38. Post-checkered hold sequence for Blue Sprint 2 is now: Finish(14:40:57) -> Yellow(14:47:39) -> Finish(14:52:24) -> Yellow(15:03:31) -> Finish(15:12:38). TWO complete Yellow round-trips inside a single hold.
poll69.strengthenedClaim: Finish is not merely non-latching; it is a state the display RE-ENTERS. Any consumer that treats the FIRST Finish as end-of-session will be wrong, and any consumer that treats a Finish->Yellow edge as 'the session resumed' will also be wrong. Only the lapsToGo 9999->0 teardown is a terminal signal, and it has still not fired at 33m48s.
poll69.flagIsTheSoleMutatingHeaderField: Across all FOUR hold edges the flag carrier changed while sessionName, clock-derived green instant, ttg (00:00:00) and lapsToGo (9999) all held. 4-for-4. During the hold the flag carrier is the only header field carrying information.
poll69.openQuestionSTILLOPEN: Whether the flag oscillation and the leaderboard rewind are coupled. This fire both moved together; the 14:52:24-14:58:34 window had a stable grid across a flag edge. Not coupled in lockstep; a shared upstream trigger is not excluded.

poll82_NORMAL_FINISH_DOES_NOT_REVERT.answersOpenQuestion: Directly answers open question #2 registered at poll 66: 'Does the same reversion happen after a NORMAL (non-caution-shortened) finish, or is it specific to a session that ended under caution with something still on track?'
poll82_NORMAL_FINISH_DOES_NOT_REVERT.result: NO REVERSION. The carrier read Finish/rgb(255,255,255) on ALL EIGHT probes spanning 3m38s of the hold (16:54:47, 16:55:11, 16:56:06, 16:56:56, 16:57:15, 16:57:43, 16:58:05, 16:58:25) and then went straight to idle at 16:59:49. No Yellow, no intermediate value.
poll82_NORMAL_FINISH_DOES_NOT_REVERT.evidentialWeight: MODERATE-TO-STRONG, and deliberately not overstated. Eight probes at 19-55s spacing cover the hold densely -- far denser than the ~3-5 min sampling that let the Blue Sprint 2 reversion hide until poll 66. The largest unobserved gap inside the hold is 55s (16:55:11->16:56:06), so a reversion would have had to be shorter than 55s AND land inside that one window to escape. Blue Sprint 2's reversion persisted at least 1m24s across three probes, so a reversion of that character would have been caught.
poll82_NORMAL_FINISH_DOES_NOT_REVERT.conclusion: The Finish -> Yellow reversion is CONDITIONAL, not a general property of the hold. The poll-66 'mostLikelyMechanism' reading -- that the carrier reports TRACK condition and goes yellow when recovery equipment is dispatched -- survives this test and is strengthened by it: Red Sprint 2 ran to full distance with a clean track at the checkered and produced no reversion, while Blue Sprint 2 ended with something still on track and did.
poll82_NORMAL_FINISH_DOES_NOT_REVERT.whatThisDoesNOTLicense: It does NOT restore Finish as a latching end-of-session marker. A controller still cannot know in advance whether a given finish is the clean kind. The poll-66 detectorConsequence stands unchanged: lapsToGo is the session-lifecycle variable, the flag carrier is an INDEPENDENT track-condition variable, and END-OF-SESSION must key on the teardown signal. This finding narrows WHEN the hazard fires; it does not remove it.
poll82_NORMAL_FINISH_DOES_NOT_REVERT.remainingOpenQuestion: Open question #1 from poll 66 -- 'does the yellow clear back to Finish, to blank, or straight to teardown?' -- is still UNANSWERED and can no longer be answered from today's data: Red Sprint 2 was the last session and produced no reversion to observe.

leaderboardCanRewindDuringHold.severity: HIGH for any results-ingestion consumer. This is the most consequential leaderboard finding of the day.
leaderboardCanRewindDuringHold.what: Between 14:49:03 and 14:52:09 the Laps column reset from the final classification (16/16/15/15/15/15/15/15/15/15/14...) down to 12, then incremented to 13 by 14:52:24 and held at 13 through 14:52:58. The leaderboard went BACKWARDS, twelve minutes after the checkered, with no teardown and no session change.

theColumnSplit.whyTheSplitIsTheKeyEvidence: It rules out a clean replay AND rules out simple corruption. #43's Diff/Gap moved 0.789 (the true final margin) -> 8.412, and #15 moved from '+1 lap' to a TIME gap of 1:11.728/1:03.316 while going from 15 laps to level-on-13 with the leader. Those are self-consistent MID-RACE values. Meanwhile every top-10 LastTime is byte-identical to the final reading and sits in the 02:5x range -- cool-down in-lap times. A grid genuinely positioned at lap 13 would show racing laps of ~01:2x-01:3x there.

leaderboardCanRewindDuringHold.conclusion: The rendered leaderboard was INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT: Laps/Diff/Gap described the race at ~lap 13 while LastTime/BestLap/BestTime described the end of the race. No single instant of the session produced this row set. It is not a snapshot of anything.
leaderboardCanRewindDuringHold.interpretationHeldLoosely: Most plausible mechanism: the timing system re-processed or re-published the session (an operator recompute, or the widget re-subscribing and rebuilding from the event stream), and the widget rendered a partially-rebuilt grid. NOT VERIFIED -- the feed exposes no signal for this, and it is inference from the column-split pattern alone. Recorded as a hypothesis, explicitly not as a finding.
whatIsNOTClaimed: Not claimed that this is a replay from lap 0.
Not claimed that the lap counter will climb back to 16.
Not claimed that the 16-lap final classification was wrong -- the 14:41:18 reading remains the best available final.
Not claimed that this happens in every session; it is n=1.
leaderboardCanRewindDuringHold.killsTheFrozenResultsHeuristicOutright: This capture task's ORIGINAL documented stop heuristic was 'results frozen across consecutive polls'. postCheckeredHoldState already showed that heuristic fires late (results mutate for minutes after the checkered). This finding is worse: results are not merely late-settling, they are NON-MONOTONIC. A consumer that latched the leaderboard on two consecutive identical polls would have latched the correct 16-lap final at 14:47:56/14:49:03 and then been contradicted by the widget itself three minutes later. Stability is not evidence of finality here, at any polling interval.
leaderboardCanRewindDuringHold.consequenceForResultsIngestion: Do NOT treat the widget's post-checkered grid as authoritative final results at any fixed delay. Either (a) wait for the teardown signal (lapsToGo 9999 -> 0) and take the LAST grid before it, accepting that this window may itself contain a rewind, or preferably (b) take final results from the API's real final-results record once apiFinalResultsSelectionRule accepts one, using the widget only as a cross-check. This is the FIRST argument today that favours the API over the widget for any purpose -- the API's records are write-once and immutable (poll 49), which is exactly the property the widget lacks here. Note the standing rule is unaffected for LIVE state: the widget remains the only authoritative source for flag and session state.
leaderboardCanRewindDuringHold.consequenceForCameraControl: Low direct impact -- camera control keys on flag and session lifecycle, not on classification. But it removes any temptation to use leaderboard stability as a session-ended proxy, reinforcing that lapsToGo 9999 -> 0 is the only sound teardown signal.

Does teardown occur while the grid is still mid-rewind, and if so does the retained idle grid hold the WRONG classification for the rest of the day? The retained idle grid has been byte-stable in every previous idle, so a rewind captured at teardown could persist for hours.
Does this reproduce on Yellow Sprint 2 / Red Sprint 2, or is it specific to a caution-shortened session whose results the timing crew may be reviewing?

leaderboardCanRewindDuringHold.samplingLesson: This was caught only because the fire took FOUR extra cheap no-sleep probes after its scheduled capture was already complete, prompted by the unexpected Yellow. The scheduled one-capture-per-fire cadence would have recorded 'hold, flag Yellow, 16 laps' and missed both the flag oscillation and the rewind entirely. Consistent with CORRECTION_poll65: repeated cheap no-sleep probes beat any single clever capture.

poll67_REWIND_STOPPED_WITHOUT_CONVERGING.stability: Byte-stable across two probes 1m49s apart: identical lap histogram {13:9, 12:7, 11:1, 10:1, 9:2}, identical top-3 LastTime values, identical row count 20, identical row order. Contrast 14:49:03->14:52:24 when Laps moved 16 -> 12 -> 13. The mutation has ceased.

whatImprovedAndWhatDidNot.improved: The Laps column is now internally ordered: values descend monotonically with finishing position (13 for P1-P9, 12 for P10-P16, 11, 10, 9, 9). At 14:52 the 12/13 mixture did not respect the order. Lap-count-vs-position coherence was recovered.
whatImprovedAndWhatDidNot.didNotImprove: The poll-66b COLUMN SPLIT persists exactly as recorded. LastTime is still the FINAL value for every top row while Laps reads 13. Verified against cautionOnsetReconstructionFromLapTimes: the leader's 02:54.458 is his LAP 16 time (fully-caution-shaped); his lap 13 was completed under GREEN and would read ~01:26. poll67_REWIND_STOPPED_WITHOUT_CONVERGING.correctedFirstPassReading: This fire's FIRST-PASS conclusion was that the grid had 'settled into a coherent lap-13 under-caution snapshot'. That was WRONG and is retracted here and in an appended JSONL correction record. The error was checking only whether Laps descended monotonically with position, and NOT cross-checking LastTime against the caution timeline already reconstructed in this file. Monotonicity of one column is not coherence of a grid. Recorded because it is the same failure mode the poll-66b entry was written to prevent, and it recurred anyway one fire later -- see trapRecurrenceUnderColdStart for the identical pattern on the API side.
poll67_REWIND_STOPPED_WITHOUT_CONVERGING.newInconsistencyFound: Rows 19 and 20 both read Laps=9, four laps down on the 13-lap leader. #08 JUSTIN JACOBS renders Diff/Gap as '+4 laps / +1 laps'; #525 DAMON DeCASTRO renders '8:28.311 / 8:28.311', a TIME gap at a four-lap deficit. Two rows at IDENTICAL lap counts disagree on the gap column's TYPE within a single rendered grid. This extends leaderboardGapColumnTypeFlips, which previously described the flip as occurring between polls: it can also occur between rows of the same grid, so a consumer cannot infer the column's type once per capture and apply it row-wise.
poll67_REWIND_STOPPED_WITHOUT_CONVERGING.conclusionRevised: The prior conclusion ('the rendered leaderboard was internally inconsistent... it is not a snapshot of anything') is UNCHANGED and now strengthened: the widget did not pass through the inconsistent state transiently on its way somewhere valid -- it CAME TO REST there. A consumer that waited for stability and then latched would latch a grid corresponding to no instant of the session, and would do so with maximum confidence, since every stability test it could run would pass.
poll67_REWIND_STOPPED_WITHOUT_CONVERGING.sharpensTheKillOfTheFrozenResultsHeurist: poll 66b argued stability is not evidence of finality. Poll 67 is the stronger form: stability is not evidence of VALIDITY either. The grid is now simultaneously stable, self-consistent on the axis a naive validator would check (position vs laps), and wrong. No test available to a leaderboard-only consumer distinguishes this from a correct final classification. The only defences are (a) capture at the checkered instant and never revise, or (b) cross-check against an independently reconstructed timeline, which is what caught it here.
openQuestionsUpdated: RESOLVED (negative): does the grid re-converge on the true final before teardown? No -- it stopped at an inconsistent lap-13 grid and held it for at least 1m49s, 17m37s into the hold.
